recipes.name: Mapo tofu (mapo doufu with beef)
recipes.description: Soft tofu simmered in a fiery red sauce of chilli bean paste, fermented black beans and crisp beef mince, finished with a numbing shower of ground Sichuan pepper.

ingredients.name: Ground Sichuan chilli or chilli flakes
Garlic shoots (suan miao) or spring onions

steps.t: Bring a saucepan of water to a bare simmer and add the teaspoon of salt. Slide in the tofu cubes and keep the water just trembling for 3 minutes; this firms the tofu so it holds its shape in the sauce and seasons it lightly. Leave the tofu in the hot water until needed.

Toast the Sichuan peppercorns in a small dry pan over low heat, shaking, for 1–2 minutes until they smell lemony and start to darken. Grind them to a powder. Mix the cornstarch with the cold water, and have the chopped bean paste, black beans, chilli, garlic and ginger ready by the stove.

Heat the wok over high heat, add 1 tablespoon of the oil and the beef. Break it up with a spatula and stir-fry for 3–4 minutes until it is brown, slightly crisp at the edges and no longer pink, and the pan is dry rather than watery.

Turn the heat down to medium-low and add the rest of the oil. Stir in the chilli bean paste and fry it gently for 1–2 minutes, until the oil turns a deep brick red and smells rich. This step, frying the paste slowly in oil, is what gives mapo tofu its glossy red sauce; on high heat the paste burns and turns bitter.
Add the black beans, ground chilli, garlic and ginger and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Pour in the water or stock, the soy sauce and sugar and bring to the boil.

Lift the tofu out of its water with a slotted spoon and slide it into the wok. Do not stir: push the tofu gently with the back of a ladle so it moves through the sauce without breaking. Simmer over medium heat for 5 minutes so it absorbs the flavour.

Stir the cornstarch mixture and add it in three additions, nudging the tofu gently after each, until the sauce thickens to a glossy coating that clings to the tofu. Add the garlic shoots or spring onions and cook for 30 seconds more, until just wilted.

Slide the tofu into a deep serving dish, scatter generously with the ground Sichuan pepper and serve straight away with plenty of steamed rice. The pepper should make your lips tingle; that numbing heat (ma la) is the point of the dish.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Chengdu home cooks usually use beef; chicken mince also works.
Pixian doubanjiang is saltier than most pastes, so taste before adding any salt.

recipes.name: Dan dan mian (dan dan noodles)
recipes.description: Wheat noodles over a sauce of sesame paste, black vinegar, soy and chilli oil, topped with crisp fried mince, greens and peanuts. Toss from the bottom so every strand is coated.

ingredients.name: Sui mi ya cai (Yibin preserved mustard greens)
Dried thin wheat noodles (or 250 g fresh)

steps.t: Make the quick chilli oil: put the chilli flakes in a heatproof bowl. Heat the 2 tablespoons of oil in a small pan over medium heat until it shimmers and a flake dropped in sizzles at once, then pour it over the chilli. It should foam and smell toasty, not burnt. Leave to cool for 5 minutes. A spoonful of ready-made chilli oil with its sediment works too.

For the topping, heat the tablespoon of oil in the wok over medium-high heat. Add the mince and break it up finely. Keep frying and stirring for 5–6 minutes, past the point where it browns, until all the liquid has gone and the mince is dark, crisp and almost crunchy; this dry-frying is what makes the topping keep and taste deeply savoury.
Add the rice wine if using, both soy sauces, the five-spice and the ya cai and stir-fry for 1 minute more, until the pan is dry again. Tip into a bowl and keep warm.
Divide the sesame paste, soy sauce, black vinegar, sugar, garlic, ground Sichuan pepper and chilli oil (with its flakes) between two wide bowls. Stir each into a thick paste.

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil and cook the noodles according to the packet, usually 3–5 minutes, until tender with a slight bite. Add the greens for the last 45 seconds so they turn bright green and just tender.

Before draining, ladle 3 tablespoons of the hot noodle water into each bowl and stir to loosen the sauce until it is smooth and pourable. Drain the noodles and greens and divide them between the bowls.

Spoon the mince over the noodles, add the greens, peanuts and spring onions and serve at once. Tell everyone to toss the noodles from the bottom of the bowl until every strand is coated in the sesame-chilli sauce before eating.

recipes.storage: Best eaten freshly made. The fried mince topping keeps 3 days in the fridge in a covered container.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the topping in a dry pan until sizzling and steaming hot; cook fresh noodles.
notes: In Chengdu dan dan noodles are a small snack bowl; these amounts make two meal-sized bowls.
Leftover sesame-chilli sauce keeps a week in the fridge.

recipes.name: Gan bian si ji dou (Sichuan dry-fried green beans)
recipes.description: Green beans fried until blistered, wrinkled and tender, then tossed with dried chillies, Sichuan pepper and garlic. This home version skips the usual pork.

ingredients.name: Green beans
ingredients.prep: trimmed and cut into 6–7 cm lengths

ingredients.name: Dried red chillies
ingredients.prep: snipped in half, seeds shaken out

ingredients.name: Sui mi ya cai (preserved mustard greens)

steps.t: Wash the beans and dry them very thoroughly with a tea towel. Any water left on them makes the oil spit and stops the skins blistering.

Heat the oil in the wok over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the beans in a single layer and fry, turning them every minute or so, for 8–10 minutes, until the skins are wrinkled and blistered with brown patches and the beans are tender when bitten. This slow frying, which drives the water out of the beans, is the 'dry-frying' (gan bian) of the name.

Lift the beans onto a plate with a slotted spoon, leaving about 1 tablespoon of oil in the wok. Lower the heat to medium, add the dried chillies and Sichuan peppercorns and stir for 20–30 seconds, until the chillies turn a deeper red and smell toasty. Take care: blackened chillies taste bitter.

Add the garlic, ginger and spring onion whites and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Return the beans with the ya cai if using, the soy sauce, sugar and a pinch of salt, and toss over high heat for 1–2 minutes until the aromatics cling to the beans.
Taste, add a little more salt if needed and serve hot as part of a shared meal with rice. Warn diners that the whole chillies are for flavour rather than for eating.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot dry wok for 1–2 minutes; the beans soften a little on standing.
notes: Restaurants deep-fry the beans; shallow-frying uses far less oil and blisters them just as well.

recipes.name: Yu xiang qie zi (fish-fragrant aubergine)
recipes.description: Silky fried aubergine in a sweet, sour and gently hot sauce of chilli bean paste, garlic, ginger and black vinegar. 'Fish-fragrant' names the seasoning; there is no fish in it.

ingredients.name: Spring onions
ingredients.prep: sliced, whites and greens kept apart

steps.t: Toss the aubergine batons with the salt in a colander and leave them for 20 minutes. Salting draws out water so the aubergine soaks up less oil and turns creamy rather than spongy. Pat the pieces dry with kitchen paper.

While the aubergine stands, stir the sugar, black vinegar, soy sauce, cornstarch and water together in a small bowl until the cornstarch dissolves. Chop the garlic and ginger and slice the spring onions.

Heat 4 tablespoons of the oil in the wok over medium-high heat until shimmering. Fry the aubergine in two batches, turning often, for 6–8 minutes per batch, until golden on the outside and so soft that a piece collapses when pressed with the spatula. Lift onto kitchen paper.

Add the last tablespoon of oil and lower the heat to medium. Fry the chilli bean paste for about 1 minute, stirring, until the oil turns red and smells rich, then add the garlic, ginger and spring onion whites and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. This sweet-sour-hot combination was traditionally used for fish, which is where the name comes from.
Stir the sauce again and pour it into the wok. Let it bubble for 30–60 seconds, until it thickens and turns glossy and translucent.

Return the aubergine and turn it gently in the sauce for 1–2 minutes until hot and well coated, taking care not to mash it. Taste: the sauce should be equally sweet and sour with a gentle heat; add a splash more vinegar or a pinch of sugar to balance it.
Scatter with the spring onion greens and serve hot with steamed rice.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: To use less oil, steam the aubergine batons for 10 minutes instead of frying, then add them to the finished sauce.

recipes.name: Pai huang gua (smashed cucumber salad)
recipes.description: Cucumbers smashed into craggy pieces, lightly salted, then dressed with garlic, black vinegar, soy, sesame oil and chilli oil. A cold, crunchy contrast to rich dishes.

steps.t: Trim the cucumbers and lay them on a board. Press down hard with the flat side of a cleaver or bash them with a rolling pin until they crack open along their length. Cut them on the diagonal into 3 cm pieces. The rough, broken surfaces soak up the dressing far better than neat slices.
Toss the cucumber with the salt in a colander and leave over a bowl for 10–15 minutes. The salt draws out water, keeping the cucumber crunchy and stopping it diluting the dressing.
Meanwhile stir the garlic, black vinegar, soy sauce, sugar, sesame oil and chilli oil together in a mixing bowl until the sugar dissolves.
Shake the cucumbers well and pour away the liquid that has collected. Add them to the dressing and toss until every piece is coated.
Pile onto a plate, scatter with coriander and sesame seeds if you like and serve cold within half an hour, while the cucumber is still crisp.

recipes.storage: Best within an hour of dressing; leftovers keep 1 day in the fridge but soften.

recipes.name: Suan la tang (hot and sour soup)
recipes.description: A thick, peppery and sharply sour soup of mushrooms, bamboo shoots and tofu with ribbons of egg. This vegetarian version gets its heat from white pepper and its sourness from black vinegar.

ingredients.name: Wood ear fungus (soaked weight) or more fresh mushrooms

steps.t: Soak the dried shiitake in 250 ml hot water and the wood ear in a separate bowl of cold water for about 20 minutes, until both are soft and pliable. Squeeze the shiitake, strain and keep the soaking liquid, cut off the stems and slice the caps thinly. Trim any hard knobs from the wood ear and slice it into strips.
Cut the tofu and bamboo shoots into matchsticks. Beat the eggs in a jug. Mix the cornstarch with the cold water in a small bowl.
Bring the stock and the strained mushroom soaking liquid to the boil in the saucepan. Add the shiitake, wood ear and bamboo shoots and simmer over medium heat for 5 minutes.

Add the tofu, both soy sauces and the sugar and simmer for 2 minutes. Stir the cornstarch mixture, then drizzle it in while stirring the soup. Simmer for 1 minute, until the soup thickens to a light, velvety body that coats the back of a spoon.

Turn the heat to its lowest. Stir the soup in a slow circle and, while it is still moving, pour in the beaten egg in a thin stream from a little height. Leave it untouched for 30 seconds so the egg sets into silky ribbons, then stir gently once.

Take the pan off the heat and stir in the black vinegar and white pepper. Adding them at the end keeps the sourness bright and the pepper hot; boiling dulls both. Taste: it should be distinctly sour and peppery. Add salt, more vinegar or more pepper to your liking.
Stir in the sesame oil, ladle into bowls and top with spring onion, and coriander and a few drops of chilli oil if you like. Serve hot.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently until steaming hot; the soup thins on standing, so stir in a little more cornstarch mixed with water if needed, and add a fresh splash of vinegar.
notes: Northern versions add strips of pork; thin strips of chicken breast, added with the tofu, make a halal-friendly meat version.

recipes.name: Qing zheng yu (Cantonese steamed fish with ginger and spring onion)
recipes.description: A whole fish steamed just until it flakes from the bone, then topped with threads of ginger and spring onion, sizzled with hot oil and dressed with sweetened soy sauce.
equipment: Wok with lid and steaming rack (or a large steamer)

ingredients.name: Whole sea bass or other firm white fish, scaled and gutted
Ginger
ingredients.prep: half sliced into coins, half cut into fine threads

ingredients.name: Spring onions
ingredients.prep: 2 cut into lengths, 2 cut into fine threads

ingredients.name: Shaoxing rice wine, to rub over the fish

steps.t: Rinse the fish inside and out and pat it completely dry. Make 2–3 diagonal cuts down to the bone on each side of the thickest part so it cooks evenly. Rub with the rice wine if using.

Cut half the ginger and two spring onions into very fine threads and drop them into a bowl of iced water; they curl and crisp while the fish cooks. Slice the rest of the ginger into coins and cut the other spring onions into lengths.

Put the steaming rack in the wok, add about 5 cm of water and bring it to a rolling boil over high heat. Lay the ginger coins and spring onion lengths on the heatproof plate and put the fish on top; raising it this way lets the steam circulate underneath.

Lower the plate onto the rack, cover and steam over high heat for 8–10 minutes for a 700 g fish. It is done when the flesh at the thickest point is opaque all the way to the bone and lifts away easily with a chopstick, and the eye has turned white. Avoid overcooking: the flesh should be just set and moist.
While the fish steams, warm the soy sauce, sugar and water in the small saucepan just until the sugar dissolves. Keep it warm.

Lift the plate out carefully, wearing oven gloves. Tip away the cloudy steaming liquid, which tastes fishy, and discard the cooked ginger and spring onion. Slide the fish onto a warm serving platter, sprinkle with white pepper and pile the drained ginger and spring onion threads on top.

Heat the oil in the small pan over high heat until it just begins to smoke, then pour it carefully over the threads; they should sizzle loudly and release their fragrance. Spoon the warm seasoned soy around (not over) the fish so the skin stays clean, add coriander and serve straight away with rice and greens.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. Take leftover flesh off the bone, refrigerate and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Steam leftovers for 3–4 minutes until piping hot; microwaving toughens the fish.
notes: For fillets, steam for 5–7 minutes depending on thickness.
Cantonese cooks judge freshness by clear eyes, red gills and firm flesh; the plain method relies on a very fresh fish.

recipes.name: Jook (Cantonese congee)
recipes.description: Rice simmered slowly with ginger until the grains burst into a silky, smooth porridge, served with soy, sesame oil, white pepper, crisp shallots and fresh toppings.

steps.t: Rinse the rice in several changes of water until it runs almost clear, then drain it well. Toss it with the teaspoon of oil and half the salt and leave for 30 minutes. Coating the grains this way helps them break down into a smooth jook; freezing the rinsed rice overnight has the same effect.
Bring the water and ginger slices to a rolling boil in the large pot. Add the rice, stir well and bring back to the boil.

Lower the heat so the congee simmers gently, set the lid ajar and cook for 75–90 minutes. Stir every 10–15 minutes, scraping the bottom of the pot so nothing sticks and scorches, and add a splash of boiling water if it thickens too fast. It is ready when the grains have burst and almost dissolved into a creamy porridge that pours slowly off a spoon.

While the congee cooks, make the crispy shallots. Put the sliced shallots and 3 tablespoons of oil in the small pan over medium-low heat and fry, stirring often, for 6–8 minutes, until evenly golden. Lift them onto kitchen paper (they crisp as they cool) and keep the fragrant oil for drizzling.
Fish out the ginger slices and season the congee with the remaining salt, tasting as you go. Plain jook should be lightly seasoned, because the toppings add salt.
Prepare the toppings: spring onion, ginger threads, coriander, crushed peanuts and diced century egg if using. Set them out with the soy sauce, sesame oil and white pepper.

Ladle the congee into deep bowls and let everyone add soy sauce, sesame oil, a pinch of white pepper, crispy shallots, a little shallot oil and whatever toppings they like. Serve very hot, traditionally with youtiao (fried dough sticks) for dipping.

recipes.storage: Congee thickens a lot as it cools. Cool quickly, refrigerate within 1 hour and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Loosen with boiling water and reheat, stirring, until steaming hot throughout.
notes: A rice-to-water ratio of about 1:12 gives a pourable Cantonese congee; use 1:8 for a thicker porridge.
For chicken jook, poach 2 boneless thighs in the congee for the last 20 minutes, then shred them back in.

recipes.name: Xi hong shi chao ji dan (tomato and egg stir-fry)
recipes.description: Soft, fluffy scrambled egg folded into tomatoes cooked down into a light sweet-sour sauce. China's best-loved home dish, made in minutes and eaten over rice.

ingredients.name: Spring onions
ingredients.prep: sliced, whites and greens kept apart

steps.t: Cut the tomatoes into wedges; for a smoother sauce, score the bases, dip them in boiling water for 20 seconds and slip off the skins first. Beat the eggs with the water and a quarter of the salt until frothy and evenly yellow.

Heat the wok over high heat until it just smokes, then add 1½ tablespoons of the oil. Pour in the eggs, let them set for 5–10 seconds, then push the set egg from the edges to the centre with a spatula so large, soft curds form. After 30–45 seconds, while the eggs are still glossy and slightly wet, tip them onto a plate.

Add the rest of the oil and the spring onion whites and stir for 10 seconds. Add the tomatoes and stir-fry over medium-high heat for 2–3 minutes, pressing some of the wedges with the spatula, until they soften and release their juice into a light sauce while some still hold their shape.

Season with the sugar and the remaining salt, and the ketchup if using. The sugar balances the acidity of the tomatoes rather than making the dish sweet. If the tomatoes are not very juicy, add 2–3 tablespoons of water to make a little more sauce.
Return the eggs to the wok and fold them through the tomatoes for about 30 seconds, just until they are hot and have soaked up some of the juice. Don't stir hard, or the curds break into crumbs.
Taste for salt, scatter over the spring onion greens and serve at once over steamed rice, spooning the tomato juices into the rice.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. Refrigerate leftovers promptly and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Use the ripest tomatoes you can find; out of season, add the ketchup for colour and depth.

recipes.name: Chicken chow mein
recipes.description: Thin egg noodles fried until crisp in places, then tossed with tender sliced chicken, bean sprouts, cabbage and spring onions in a savoury oyster and soy sauce.
equipment: Wok or very large frying pan

ingredients.name: Thin dried egg noodles (chow mein noodles)

steps.t: Toss the sliced chicken with the soy sauce, cornstarch and oil until each piece is lightly coated, and leave for 10 minutes. The thin starch coating keeps the meat juicy over high heat.

Cook the noodles in a large pot of boiling water for 1 minute less than the packet says, usually 2–3 minutes, until just tender. Drain, rinse under cold water and shake very dry, then spread them out on a tray for a few minutes. Dry noodles crisp; wet ones steam and clump.
Stir the oyster sauce, both soy sauces, sugar, water and white pepper together in a small bowl. Put the vegetables by the stove: once the wok is hot everything moves quickly.

Heat the wok over high heat until smoking and add 1 tablespoon of the oil. Spread the chicken out in one layer, leave it for 1 minute to sear, then stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until cooked through with no pink inside. Tip onto a plate.

Add another 1½ tablespoons of oil and swirl. Add the noodles and spread them over the base of the wok. Leave them alone for about 2 minutes, until the underside is golden and crisp, then turn them over in sections and cook for 1–2 minutes more.

Push the noodles to one side, add the last of the oil and stir-fry the garlic, carrot and cabbage for 1 minute. Add the bean sprouts, spring onions and chicken, pour over the sauce and toss everything together with tongs or chopsticks for 1–2 minutes, until the noodles are evenly coloured and the vegetables are hot but still crunchy.
Turn off the heat, drizzle with the sesame oil, toss once more and serve straight away.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Hong Kong-style crispy chow mein fries the noodles into a single golden cake and pours the stir-fry over it; use an extra tablespoon of oil and don't break the noodles up.

recipes.name: Beef and broccoli (gai lan chao niu rou)
recipes.description: Silky, tender slices of beef and bright, crisp broccoli or Chinese broccoli stir-fried in a glossy oyster sauce. Velveting the beef keeps it soft over high heat.

ingredients.name: Flank or sirloin steak
ingredients.prep: sliced 5 mm thick across the grain

steps.t: For thin slices, chill the beef in the freezer for 20 minutes, then slice across the grain. Massage the soy sauce, bicarbonate of soda and water into the beef until absorbed, then mix in the cornstarch and finally the oil. Leave for 15 minutes. This is velveting: the bicarbonate softens the meat and the starch protects it, giving the smooth texture of Cantonese restaurant beef.
Bring a saucepan of salted water to the boil. Blanch the broccoli for 1–1½ minutes (gai lan for 2 minutes), until bright green and just crisp-tender, then drain well and shake dry.
Stir the oyster sauce, both soy sauces, sugar, cornstarch, water and sesame oil together in a small bowl.

Heat the wok over high heat until it smokes and add 1½ tablespoons of the oil. Spread the beef in a single layer and leave it for 30–60 seconds to sear, then stir-fry for about 1 minute more, until no longer red on the outside but still slightly pink inside. Tip it onto a plate; it finishes cooking later.
Add the remaining oil, the garlic and ginger and stir for 15 seconds until fragrant. Add the broccoli and toss for 1 minute; splash in the rice wine around the edge of the wok if using.

Stir the sauce and pour it in. Let it bubble for 30 seconds until it turns glossy, then return the beef and its juices and toss for 30–60 seconds, until every piece is coated and the beef is just cooked through.
Serve straight away with steamed rice. Stir-fried beef toughens as it sits, so bring it to the table as soon as it is done.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Cong you bing (scallion pancakes)
recipes.description: Flaky, chewy flatbreads layered with spring onion and a savoury oil paste, coiled and pan-fried until crisp and golden. Made with a hot-water dough for tenderness.

ingredients.name: Spring onions
ingredients.prep: very thinly sliced and patted dry

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt in a bowl. Pour in the boiling water while stirring with chopsticks until it forms shaggy flakes, then add the cold water and bring it together by hand. Knead for about 5 minutes, until smooth and as soft as an earlobe. Cover and rest for 30 minutes. Hot water partly cooks the starch, so the pancakes stay tender and chewy rather than tough.
Stir the oil, flour, salt and pepper together into a loose paste. This oil paste (you su) keeps the layers separate so the pancakes turn flaky.

Divide the dough into 4 pieces. On a lightly oiled surface, roll one piece into a thin rectangle about 30 x 20 cm. Brush with a quarter of the oil paste right to the edges and scatter with a quarter of the spring onion.

Roll the dough up tightly from a long side into a rope, then coil the rope into a snail shape and tuck the end underneath. Repeat with the rest and leave the coils to rest under a cloth for 10 minutes, so the gluten relaxes and they roll out without springing back.
Press each coil flat with your palm, then roll it gently into a round about 18 cm across and 5 mm thick. A few spring onions poking through is fine.

Heat 2 teaspoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat. Fry one pancake, covered, for 3 minutes until the underside is deep golden, then turn it, uncovered, and fry 3 minutes more, adding a little more oil around the edge, until both sides are crisp and the pancake has puffed.

While it is still in the pan, push the edges towards the centre with two spatulas to scrunch the pancake; this breaks open the layers and makes it flakier. Repeat with the remaining pancakes, keeping the cooked ones warm in a low oven.
Cut into wedges and serve hot with a dip of soy sauce and black vinegar, or with chilli oil.

recipes.storage: Wrap cooled pancakes and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Uncooked coils freeze well between sheets of baking paper for 1 month; fry from frozen over slightly lower heat.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes per side until crisp again.

recipes.name: Cong you ban mian (Shanghai scallion oil noodles)
recipes.description: Thin wheat noodles tossed in a dark, glossy sauce of soy sauce and sugar cooked in oil that has been slowly infused with spring onions until they turn crisp and sweet.

ingredients.name: Spring onions
ingredients.prep: cut into 8 cm lengths, whites and greens kept apart

steps.t: Cut the spring onions into lengths and pat them completely dry; water makes the oil spit and stops them crisping. Stir the two soy sauces and the sugar together in a small bowl.
Put the oil and the spring onion whites in the cold wok and set it over medium-low heat. Fry gently for 5 minutes, until the whites start to soften and bubble steadily.

Add the green parts and keep frying over medium-low heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring now and then, until all the spring onions have shrunk and turned deep brown and crisp but not black. Low heat matters here: hurried, the onions burn and turn bitter before they release their sweetness into the oil.

Lift the crisp spring onions out onto a plate. Pour the soy and sugar mixture into the hot oil; it will bubble up fiercely. Stir for 30–60 seconds, until the sugar has dissolved and the sauce looks slightly syrupy, then take it off the heat. This is the scallion oil sauce.
Meanwhile cook the noodles in plenty of boiling water according to the packet, usually 3–4 minutes, until tender with a little bite. Drain, keeping a splash of the cooking water.

Divide the noodles between two bowls and spoon 2–3 tablespoons of the sauce over each. Toss with chopsticks until every strand is glossy and evenly brown, adding a spoonful of noodle water if they feel sticky. Top with the crisp spring onions and serve hot, with a fried egg if you like.

recipes.storage: Keep leftover scallion oil sauce in a clean jar in the fridge for up to 2 weeks. Cook noodles fresh.
notes: The sauce is also excellent spooned over rice, steamed greens or a fried egg.

recipes.name: Jiaozi (beef and Chinese cabbage dumplings)
recipes.description: Handmade boiled dumplings with juicy beef and napa cabbage filling, folded into crescents and served with a garlicky black vinegar dip. A Lunar New Year essential in northern China.

ingredients.name: Hot water, for the pepper water

steps.t: Make the dough: mix the flour and salt, then add the water gradually, stirring with chopsticks into small flakes. Bring together and knead for 8–10 minutes, until smooth and elastic: a finger pressed into it should leave a dent that slowly springs back. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Toss the chopped cabbage with the teaspoon of salt and leave for 15 minutes, then squeeze it very dry in a clean cloth, a handful at a time. Removing the water keeps the filling from turning soggy and tearing the wrappers. Steep the Sichuan peppercorns in the hot water for 10 minutes, then strain and cool this pepper water.

Put the beef, ginger, soy sauce, white pepper and salt in a bowl. Stir hard in one direction with chopsticks while adding the pepper water a spoonful at a time, and keep beating for 2–3 minutes until the meat has absorbed all the liquid and turned sticky and springy. Beating in liquid this way is what makes northern dumplings juicy. Fold in the cabbage, spring onions, sesame oil and neutral oil.

Roll the dough into ropes about 2.5 cm thick and cut into 40 pieces of about 15 g. Dust with flour, press each one flat, then roll it into an 8 cm round, turning it a little after each stroke so the edges end up thinner than the centre.

Put a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre of a wrapper and fold it in half. Pinch the top closed, then make 3–4 small pleats along one side, pressing each one against the flat back side, to form a crescent. Seal the edges firmly and set the dumplings on a floured tray, not touching. Keep the unused dough and wrappers covered with a cloth.

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil. Add 12–15 dumplings and stir gently so they don't stick to the bottom. When the water returns to the boil, add 125 ml of cold water; repeat twice more. The three cold-water additions let the filling cook through without the skins bursting. After 7–8 minutes the dumplings float and look puffed; cut one open to check the beef is no longer pink.
While the dumplings cook, stir the black vinegar, soy sauce, garlic and chilli oil (if using) together for the dip.

Lift the dumplings out with a slotted spoon, cook the remaining batches the same way and serve hot with the dip. Northern families drink a little of the cooking water afterwards, said to aid digestion.

recipes.storage: Freeze uncooked dumplings on the floured tray until hard, then bag them; cook from frozen, adding 2 minutes. Cooked leftovers keep 2 days in the fridge.
recipes.reheating: Pan-fry cooked leftovers in a little oil until crisp underneath and steaming hot throughout.
notes: Ready-made round dumpling wrappers save about 30 minutes; you need about 40.
Chicken mince works the same way; add an extra tablespoon of oil because it is leaner.

recipes.name: Yang rou chuan (Xinjiang cumin lamb skewers)
recipes.description: Cubes of lamb and lamb fat threaded on skewers, grilled over high heat and showered with toasted cumin, chilli and salt. The smoky street food of Urumqi and night markets across China.
equipment: Barbecue, grill pan or overhead grill

steps.t: If using bamboo skewers, soak them in water for 30 minutes so they don't burn. Cut the lamb into 2 cm cubes, keeping the fatty pieces separate; the fat bastes the meat as it grills.

Mix the grated onion (with its juice), oil and half a teaspoon of salt, toss the lamb in it and leave for at least 1 hour in the fridge, or overnight. The onion juice tenderises the meat and softens the gamey flavour.

Toast the cumin seeds in the small dry pan over medium heat for 1–2 minutes, shaking, until they darken slightly and smell nutty. Grind half of them coarsely, then mix all the cumin with the chilli, salt and the Sichuan pepper and sesame seeds if using.
Wipe most of the onion off the lamb and thread 4–5 cubes tightly onto each skewer, putting a piece of fat between the lean cubes.

Heat the barbecue, grill pan or grill until very hot. Grill the skewers for 8–10 minutes in total, turning every 2–3 minutes and sprinkling generously with the spice mix each time you turn them, so it toasts onto the sizzling fat. They are done when the edges are charred and the meat is browned outside; cook to pink and juicy or well done, as you prefer.
Rest for 2 minutes, give a final sprinkle of spice mix and serve hot, with flatbread and thinly sliced raw onion.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat briefly under a hot grill; long reheating makes them tough.

recipes.name: Da pan ji (Xinjiang big plate chicken)
recipes.description: Bone-in chicken and potatoes braised with dried chillies, Sichuan pepper and warm spices, finished with green peppers and served on a big platter of wide noodles that soak up the sauce.
equipment: Large wok or wide casserole with lid

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 5 cm chunks

ingredients.name: Wide flat noodles (dried belt noodles or pappardelle)

steps.t: Pat the chicken pieces dry. Cut the potatoes into large chunks and keep them in a bowl of water so they don't brown. Cut the peppers and onion into chunks and set out the whole spices, ginger and garlic.

Put the oil and sugar in the wok over medium heat. Stir until the sugar melts and turns a clear amber caramel, 1–2 minutes; watch closely, because it burns quickly. This caramel gives the dish its glossy red-brown colour.
Add the chicken straight away, turn the heat to high and fry for 5–6 minutes, turning often, until every piece is coated in caramel and browned at the edges.

Add the dried chillies, Sichuan peppercorns, star anise, cinnamon, bay leaves, ginger and garlic and stir for 1 minute until fragrant. Add the chilli bean paste and stir for another minute, until the oil turns red.
Pour in both soy sauces and the water, which should just cover the chicken. Bring to the boil, cover and simmer over medium-low heat for 20 minutes.
Drain the potatoes, add them to the pan, cover again and simmer for 15–20 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the chicken is cooked through, with clear juices at the bone.
While the chicken braises, cook the noodles in a large pot of boiling water until just tender. Drain and toss with a few drops of oil so they don't stick.

Uncover the chicken, add the peppers and onion and boil hard for 3–4 minutes, until the peppers are just tender and the sauce has reduced to a thick, glossy gravy. Taste for salt. Spread the noodles over a large platter, pile the chicken and potatoes on top and pour over all the sauce. Fish out the whole spices as you eat.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: In Xinjiang the noodles are hand-pulled belt noodles (kemian) laid under the chicken once most of it has been eaten; serving them together is the usual home shortcut.

recipes.name: Yangzhou chao fan (Yangzhou fried rice)
recipes.description: The banquet-style fried rice of Yangzhou: separate, egg-coated grains with prawns, chicken, shiitake, peas and carrot, seasoned with salt and white pepper rather than soy so it stays golden.

ingredients.name: Eggs
ingredients.prep: beaten with a pinch of salt

ingredients.name: Cooked ham or char siu, diced (the classic addition)
Shaoxing rice wine, for the prawns

steps.t: Use rice cooked the day before and chilled: fresh rice is too moist and turns mushy. Break up the clumps with wet fingers so the grains are loose. Soak the shiitake in hot water for 20 minutes, squeeze dry and dice. Pat the prawns and chicken dry.

Bring a small pan of water to the boil and blanch the carrot and peas for 1 minute, then drain well. Blanching means they only need warming through in the wok, so the rice is not overcooked while they soften.

Heat the wok over high heat until smoking and add 1 tablespoon of the oil. Stir-fry the chicken for 2 minutes, then add the prawns (and the rice wine, if using) and stir-fry for 1–2 minutes more, until the prawns are pink and opaque and the chicken is white throughout. Tip onto a plate.

Add the remaining oil and pour in the eggs. After about 10 seconds, when the edges have set but the top is still runny, add the rice and toss vigorously, pressing and turning, for 3–4 minutes. The half-cooked egg coats the grains (the Yangzhou 'gold-wrapped silver'), and the rice is ready when it is hot, separate and jumps in the wok.

Add the shiitake, carrot and peas, and the ham if using, and toss for 1 minute. Return the chicken and prawns, season with the salt and white pepper, then drizzle the stock around the hot edge of the wok so it sizzles and steams into the rice. Toss for 1 minute more.
Add the spring onions, toss for a few seconds, taste for salt and serve immediately.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 1 hour of cooking and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Yangzhou fried rice is traditionally made with ham or char siu; this version uses chicken so it suits a halal kitchen, with ham as an optional extra.

recipes.name: Xiao chao huang niu rou (Hunan stir-fried beef with chillies)
recipes.description: Thin slices of tender beef stir-fried hot with blistered fresh green and red chillies, garlic, fermented black beans, celery and plenty of coriander. Fiery, fragrant and made for rice.

steps.t: Massage the beef with the soy sauce, bicarbonate of soda and water until absorbed, then mix in the cornstarch and finally the oil. Leave for 15 minutes while you prepare the vegetables; the coating keeps the beef tender over fierce heat.
Slice the chillies, cut the celery and coriander into lengths and slice the garlic and ginger. Hunan cooking uses whole fresh chillies generously; for less heat, scrape out some seeds.

Heat the wok over medium heat, add the chillies with a pinch of salt and no oil, and press and toss them for 2–3 minutes until blistered, softened and smelling smoky. This dry-frying drives off water and concentrates their flavour. Tip them out.

Add 2 tablespoons of the oil and heat over high heat until it smokes. Spread the beef in one layer, leave it for 30–60 seconds to sear, then stir-fry for about 1 minute until browned outside but still a little pink. Tip it out.

Add the remaining oil with the garlic, ginger and black beans and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the celery and stir-fry for 1 minute, then return the chillies and beef, add both soy sauces and toss over high heat for 1 minute until everything is glossy and the beef is just cooked through.
Toss in the coriander for 10 seconds, add the splash of vinegar if using, taste for salt and serve straight away with plenty of steamed rice.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Jianbing (savoury egg crêpe)
recipes.description: A thin grain crêpe cooked with an egg spread over it, brushed with sweet bean and chilli sauces, then folded around spring onion, coriander and a crisp fried wafer. China's favourite breakfast on the go.
equipment: Large non-stick frying pan (28 cm or more)

ingredients.name: Wonton wrappers, for the crisp wafers

steps.t: Whisk the flour, cornmeal, five-spice, salt and water into a smooth batter with the consistency of single cream. Leave it to rest for 10 minutes so the flour hydrates and the crêpe spreads thinly without tearing.

Make the crisp wafers (bao cui): heat the 3 tablespoons of oil in the small pan over medium-high heat and fry the wonton wrappers one at a time for 20–30 seconds per side, until puffed, blistered and golden. Drain on kitchen paper; they crisp as they cool. Loosen the sweet bean sauce with 1 teaspoon of water.

Heat the large pan over medium-low heat and wipe it with 1 teaspoon of oil. Pour in half the batter and immediately spread it into a thin, even round with the back of a ladle or a spatula, working from the centre outwards. Cook for about 1 minute, until the surface looks dry and set.

Crack an egg onto the crêpe, break the yolk and spread the egg over the whole surface. Scatter with half the spring onion, coriander and sesame seeds and cook for 1–2 minutes, until the egg has set completely and the underside of the crêpe is lightly browned.

Slide the spatula under the crêpe and flip it over in one go. Brush the plain side with half the sweet bean sauce and half the chilli sauce, then lay three crisp wafers (and a lettuce leaf if using) across the middle.

Fold the sides of the crêpe over the wafers to make a rectangular parcel, press gently and cook for 30 seconds more. Cut it in half and serve straight away while the wafers still crackle. Repeat with the remaining batter and filling.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight from the pan; the wafers soften within minutes. The batter keeps 1 day, covered, in the fridge.
notes: Street vendors in Tianjin fold in a youtiao (fried dough stick) instead of wafers; Shandong jianbing is a thinner, larger crêpe made with millet or corn and rolled around spring onions.

recipes.name: Yan ju ji (Hakka salt-baked chicken)
recipes.description: A whole chicken rubbed with salt and sand ginger, wrapped in paper and baked buried in hot coarse salt until the meat is silky and fragrant. Served with a sizzling ginger and spring onion oil.
equipment: Large heavy casserole (Dutch oven) with lid

ingredients.name: Sand ginger powder (sha jiang fen), or ground ginger
Coarse salt, for the crust (not eaten; can be reused once)

steps.t: Pat the chicken dry inside and out. Mix the salt and sand ginger powder (and the rice wine, if using) and rub it all over the skin and inside the cavity. Put the ginger slices and knotted spring onions in the cavity. Leave the chicken uncovered in the fridge for at least 2 hours, or overnight, to season the meat and dry the skin.
Heat the oven to 200 °C. Wrap the chicken snugly in two layers of baking parchment and tie it with string. The paper keeps the salt crust off the meat while letting the heat through.

Put the coarse salt in the dry wok over high heat and stir-fry it for about 10 minutes, until it is very hot and a drop of water flicked onto it hisses instantly. Hot salt starts cooking the chicken at once and holds an even heat around it.

Spread about a third of the hot salt over the base of the casserole, set the wrapped chicken on it breast side up and pour the rest of the salt over and around it until it is completely buried. Put on the lid.

Bake for 60–70 minutes. Dig away a little salt, pierce the paper and check the thickest part of the thigh with a thermometer: it must read 74 °C, and the juices should run clear. If not, re-cover and bake 10 minutes more.

While the chicken bakes, put the chopped ginger, spring onions and salt in a heatproof bowl. Heat the oil in a small pan until it just begins to smoke and pour it over; it should sizzle fiercely. Stir and leave to cool.

Lift the parcel out, brush off the salt and unwrap the chicken over a tray to catch the juices. Rest it for 10 minutes, then chop it through the bone into pieces Cantonese-style, or carve it. Serve warm or at room temperature with the ginger and spring onion oil and steamed rice.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Usually eaten warm or at room temperature; to serve hot, steam pieces for 5–8 minutes until steaming hot throughout.
notes: Sand ginger (shan nai, a relative of galangal) gives the dish its distinctive perfume; Asian grocers sell it as a powder.
Many Hakka home cooks steam the paper-wrapped, salt-rubbed chicken for about 45 minutes instead; the flavour is similar and it uses no salt crust.

recipes.name: Hong Kong milk tea (nai cha)
recipes.description: Very strong black tea 'pulled' through a fine cloth strainer until smooth, then poured over evaporated milk. Silky, bittersweet and the heart of every Hong Kong café breakfast.
equipment: Fine cloth tea strainer or very fine sieve

ingredients.name: Very strong black tea (from about 16 g / 4 tbsp loose Ceylon-style leaves brewed in 500 ml water)
Sweetened condensed milk, instead of sugar and some of the evaporated milk

steps.t: Put the loose tea leaves and 500 ml water in a saucepan and bring to the boil. Lower the heat and simmer gently for 5 minutes; Hong Kong milk tea is deliberately much stronger than ordinary tea so it can stand up to the evaporated milk.

Pull the tea: pour it through the cloth strainer into the second pan, holding the strainer high so the tea falls a long way, then pour it back through into the first pan. Repeat 4–6 times. Pulling aerates the tea and smooths out the bitterness, which is why it is called 'silk stocking' tea.
Return the tea to low heat and let it steep for 3–5 minutes more, without boiling, then strain it a final time. It should be very dark and slightly astringent.
Warm the cups with hot water, then tip it out. Pour 60 ml of evaporated milk into each cup and stir in sugar to taste.

Pour the hot tea over the milk from a little height so it mixes itself; it should turn a smooth caramel-bronze colour. Serve hot, or chill the tea and pour it over ice with the milk for iced milk tea.

recipes.storage: Best freshly made. The strong tea base keeps 2 days in the fridge for iced milk tea; add the milk when serving.
notes: Café blends mix several Ceylon teas; a strong breakfast blend or loose Ceylon tea works well at home.
With condensed milk instead of sugar it becomes cha chow, a richer, sweeter cup.

recipes.name: Sai do si (Hong Kong French toast)
recipes.description: Thick white bread sandwiched with peanut butter, soaked in egg and fried until puffed and golden, then topped with a slab of butter and golden syrup. The indulgent café classic.

ingredients.name: Thick-cut white bread (4 slices, about 2.5 cm thick)

steps.t: Spread the peanut butter over two slices of bread, right to the edges, and top with the other two slices. Press firmly so they hold together. Cafés trim off the crusts; do so if you like.
Beat the eggs and milk together in a shallow dish until evenly mixed.
Heat about 1 cm of oil in the frying pan over medium heat to about 170 °C, when a cube of bread browns in 30 seconds. Too hot and the outside burns before the egg inside the bread cooks.
Dip one sandwich into the egg for about 10 seconds per side, and roll the edges in it too, so it is completely coated and has soaked up some egg without falling apart.
Fry for 2–3 minutes per side, until deep golden, puffed and crisp, with the egg set all round the edges. Drain on kitchen paper and repeat with the second sandwich.
Set each toast on a warm plate, put a slab of butter on top and pour over the golden syrup so it runs down the sides as the butter melts. Cut into quarters and serve at once, with Hong Kong milk tea.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; it doesn't keep well.
notes: For a lighter version, fry in 2 tablespoons of oil in a non-stick pan; it will be flatter but still crisp.

recipes.name: Dan tat (Hong Kong egg tarts)
recipes.description: Crumbly butter pastry cases filled with a smooth, glossy egg custard and baked until just set with a gentle wobble. Best eaten warm from the oven.
equipment: 12-hole tart or muffin tin (or egg tart moulds)

ingredients.name: Egg
ingredients.prep: beaten; half for the pastry, half for the custard

steps.t: Make the pastry: mix the flour and icing sugar, then rub in the cold butter with your fingertips until it looks like fine breadcrumbs. Add half the beaten egg and bring it together into a soft dough without kneading, which would make it tough. Flatten into a disc, wrap and chill for 30 minutes.
For the custard, stir the sugar into the hot water until completely dissolved, then leave this syrup to cool to room temperature. Hot syrup would scramble the eggs.

Whisk the 3 eggs and the remaining beaten egg gently, so you don't create foam, then whisk in the evaporated milk, the cooled syrup and the vanilla if using. Strain twice through a fine sieve and skim off any bubbles. A strained custard bakes to the glassy-smooth surface Hong Kong tarts are known for.

Heat the oven to 200 °C. Roll the pastry out to 3 mm thick and cut 12 rounds of 9 cm, re-rolling the scraps once. Press each round into the tin, pushing the pastry up the sides so it stands just above the rim. Chill for 10 minutes so it holds its shape in the oven.
Pour the custard into the cases until they are 85–90% full. Overfilled tarts spill and the custard puffs up.

Bake for 10 minutes at 200 °C to set the pastry, then lower the oven to 180 °C and bake for 12–15 minutes more, until the pastry is golden and the custard is set at the edges with a slight wobble in the centre. If the custard starts to puff up and dome, open the oven door a crack for a minute: it should stay flat and glossy.
Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, then ease the tarts out with a small knife. Serve warm, ideally within a few hours of baking.

recipes.storage: Keep covered in the fridge and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a 160 °C oven for 5 minutes to crisp the pastry.
notes: Many Hong Kong bakeries use a flaky puff-style pastry instead; 320 g ready-rolled puff pastry, cut into rounds and pressed into the tin, works with the same custard.

recipes.name: Wonton mein (prawn wonton noodle soup)
recipes.description: Silky prawn wontons and springy thin egg noodles in a clear, gingery broth with greens and chives. Wontons go in first, under the noodles, the way Hong Kong noodle shops serve them.

ingredients.name: Fish sauce (stands in for dried flounder)
Thin dried egg noodles (or 400 g fresh wonton noodles)

steps.t: Pat the prawns dry. Chop half of them finely to a paste and the other half into coarse pieces. Mix both with the egg white, cornstarch, sesame oil, soy sauce, sugar, salt and pepper, then stir hard in one direction, lifting and slapping the mixture against the bowl, for 1–2 minutes until sticky and springy. This gives the bouncy bite of good wontons. Chill for 15 minutes.

Put the broth ingredients except the salt in a saucepan, bring to a simmer and cook gently for 15 minutes while you fold the wontons. Taste and add salt; it should be well seasoned but clear and light. Keep it hot.

To fold, put a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre of a wrapper and dab the edges with water. Fold it into a triangle, pressing out the air, then bring the two side corners together and pinch them. Alternatively, gather the wrapper loosely around the filling and squeeze at the neck, leaving a frilly 'goldfish tail'. Keep folded wontons under a damp cloth.

Bring two large pots of water to the boil. Cook the wontons in one, in batches, for 3–4 minutes, until they float and the prawns show pink through the wrapper. Lift them out with a slotted spoon into the serving bowls.

In the other pot, blanch the greens for about 1 minute, until bright green, and lift them out. Cook the noodles for 30–60 seconds if fresh or 2–3 minutes if dried, until just tender and springy. Drain, rinse briefly under cold water, then dip back into the hot water for a few seconds; noodle shops do this so they stay springy rather than soft.
Arrange the noodles on top of the wontons in each bowl. Keeping the wontons underneath stops the noodles soaking up broth and turning soft.
Ladle the hot broth over, add the greens and scatter with chives. Serve at once with red vinegar and chilli oil on the side.

recipes.storage: Freeze uncooked wontons on a tray, then bag them, for up to 1 month; cook from frozen for 5 minutes. The broth keeps 3 days in the fridge.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Yeung chi gam lo (mango pomelo sago)
recipes.description: A chilled, creamy mango soup with coconut and evaporated milk, filled with tiny chewy sago pearls and topped with fresh mango and bursting pomelo sacs.

ingredients.name: Ripe mango flesh (from about 2 large mangoes)

steps.t: Bring 1 litre of water to a rolling boil, add the sago and stir so it doesn't stick together. Boil for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, then turn off the heat, cover and leave for 10 minutes until the pearls are completely translucent with no white dot in the middle.
Drain the sago in a sieve and rinse it under cold running water to wash away the excess starch, which would make the dessert gluey. Leave it in a bowl of cold water while you make the mango base.

Cut the cheeks off the mangoes and scoop out the flesh. Dice about a third into 1 cm cubes for the topping. Blend the rest with the evaporated milk, coconut milk, sugar and cold water until completely smooth. Taste: sweetness depends on the mangoes, so add more sugar or water as needed.
Peel the pomelo, remove the pith and membranes and break the flesh into small individual sacs.
Drain the sago and stir most of it into the mango base. Chill for at least 1 hour, until very cold.
Ladle into bowls and top each with diced mango, pomelo sacs and the remaining sago. Serve cold.

recipes.storage: Keep covered in the fridge and eat within 1 day; the sago firms up as it stands.
notes: Pomelo is less juicy than grapefruit and breaks into firm sacs; pink grapefruit is the usual substitute but is more sour.

recipes.name: Hong shao niu rou mian (Taiwanese braised beef noodle soup)
recipes.description: Chunks of beef shank braised for hours in a rich, spiced soy broth with chilli bean paste and tomato, served over thick wheat noodles with bok choy and pickled mustard greens.

ingredients.name: Taiwanese rice wine (mijiu) or Shaoxing wine

steps.t: Put the beef in a pot, cover with cold water and bring to the boil. Boil for 3–5 minutes, until grey foam rises, then drain, rinse each piece under warm water and wash the pot. Blanching removes blood and impurities so the broth ends up clean-tasting rather than murky.

Heat the oil in the clean pot over medium heat. Fry the ginger, garlic and spring onion lengths for 2 minutes, until fragrant and lightly golden. Add the chilli bean paste and stir for 1 minute until the oil turns red, then add the star anise, cinnamon, bay leaves, Sichuan pepper and dried chillies and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the beef and turn it in the aromatics for 2 minutes. Pour in the rice wine (if using), both soy sauces and the sugar and stir for 2 minutes more, until the beef is glazed and dark.

Add the tomatoes and the water and bring to the boil, skimming off any foam. Cover and simmer over low heat for 2–2½ hours, until a chopstick slides easily into the beef and the tendons have turned soft and gelatinous.

Fish out the whole spices and the spent aromatics (or strain the broth and return the beef). Taste the broth: it should be rich, savoury and gently spicy. Add salt, a splash of soy or a little water to balance it.
Shortly before serving, cook the noodles in a large pot of boiling water according to the packet, until tender but still chewy. Blanch the bok choy in the same water for 1 minute.
Divide the noodles between four large bowls, ladle over the hot broth and beef and add the bok choy. Top with spring onion, and coriander and pickled mustard greens if you like, and serve very hot.

recipes.storage: The beef and broth keep 3 days in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer; the flavour improves overnight. Cook noodles fresh.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: A pressure cooker cuts the braise to about 45 minutes at high pressure.

recipes.name: San bei ji (three-cup chicken)
recipes.description: Chicken braised with a mountain of ginger, whole garlic cloves and sesame oil in soy sauce until sticky and glossy, then tossed with fresh basil. Rice wine is traditional; stock works too.
equipment: Clay pot, wok or heavy frying pan with lid

ingredients.name: Chicken thighs, boneless (or 900 g bone-in pieces)
Toasted sesame oil (black sesame oil if you have it)
Taiwanese rice wine (mijiu), instead of the stock

steps.t: Pat the chicken pieces dry. Slice the ginger into thick coins, peel the garlic and slice the chillies.

Put the sesame oil and ginger in the clay pot or wok over medium-low heat and fry gently for 4–5 minutes, until the ginger slices curl at the edges, turn golden brown and smell sweet. Keep the heat moderate: sesame oil scorches and turns bitter on high heat.
Add the garlic cloves and fry for 2–3 minutes more, turning them, until golden on all sides.
Turn the heat up to medium-high, add the chicken and fry for about 5 minutes, turning, until the pieces are lightly browned all over.
Add both soy sauces, the sugar, the stock (or rice wine, if using) and the chillies. Bring to the boil, cover and cook over medium-low heat for 10 minutes.

Uncover, raise the heat to high and stir for 4–6 minutes as the sauce bubbles and reduces to a sticky, dark glaze that coats the chicken. Check a thick piece: it should be cooked through with no pink.
Take the pot off the heat, fold in the basil and cover for 30 seconds so it wilts in the residual heat and releases its aroma. Serve straight from the pot, still sizzling, with steamed rice.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: The name refers to the original equal cups of sesame oil, soy sauce and rice wine; modern home cooks use far less of each.
The ginger slices and garlic cloves are meant to be eaten; they turn soft and sweet.

recipes.name: Yan su ji (Taiwanese popcorn chicken)
recipes.description: Bite-sized chicken marinated in soy, garlic and five-spice, coated in starch and double-fried until shatteringly crisp, then tossed with fried basil and a peppery seasoning salt.

ingredients.name: Coarse sweet potato starch (or potato starch)

steps.t: Mix the chicken with the soy sauce, garlic, ginger, five-spice, white pepper and sugar (and the rice wine, if using). Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 30 minutes, or up to 4 hours.
Stir the seasoning salt ingredients together in a small bowl. Make sure the basil leaves are completely dry; any water will make the hot oil spit violently.
Pour the oil into the deep pan, filling it no more than a third full, and heat it to 170 °C.

Toss the chicken in the starch, pressing it on so every piece is well coated. Leave for 5 minutes until the coating looks slightly damp; this hydrated starch fries into the craggy, crunchy crust night-market chicken is known for.

Fry the chicken in batches for 4–5 minutes, until pale golden and cooked through (74 °C in the centre of a large piece). Lift onto the wire rack with the slotted spoon. Don't crowd the pan, or the oil cools and the crust turns greasy.

Raise the oil temperature to 190 °C and fry all the chicken again for about 1 minute, until deep golden and very crisp. This second fry drives out moisture from the crust so it stays crunchy. Drain on the rack.

Standing back, drop the basil into the hot oil for 5–10 seconds until it turns translucent and crisp, then lift it out. Toss the chicken and basil with the seasoning salt in a large bowl and serve hot, with toothpicks, the way the night-market stalls do.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven or air fryer for 5–6 minutes until piping hot.

recipes.name: Di gua zhou (Taiwanese sweet potato congee)
recipes.description: A loose, gently sweet rice porridge cooked with chunks of golden sweet potato. Taiwanese families eat it plain, with small savoury side dishes such as pickles, eggs and stir-fried greens.

ingredients.name: Sweet potatoes (yellow or orange-fleshed)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 3 cm chunks

ingredients.name: Taiwanese pickled cucumbers (jiang gua), to serve

steps.t: Rinse the rice in several changes of water until the water runs nearly clear, then drain. Peel the sweet potatoes, cut them into chunks and rinse off the surface starch.
Bring the water to the boil in the pot. Add the rice, stir to stop it sticking to the base and bring back to the boil.
Lower the heat so it simmers gently, set the lid ajar and cook for 20 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes or so and scraping the bottom of the pot.
Add the sweet potato and simmer for 20–25 minutes more, stirring occasionally, until the sweet potato is completely tender and its edges have started to melt into the porridge, turning it pale gold.

Check the texture: Taiwanese congee is looser than Cantonese jook, with whole, swollen grains in plenty of silky liquid. Add a splash of boiling water if it has thickened too much, and a pinch of salt if you like.

Serve hot or warm in bowls alongside small savoury dishes: pickled cucumbers, a fried or salted egg, stir-fried greens, fermented tofu or peanuts. The plain, sweet congee is the backdrop for these salty sides.

recipes.storage: Cool quickly, refrigerate within 1 hour and eat within 2 days; it thickens as it stands.
recipes.reheating: Loosen with boiling water and reheat, stirring, until steaming hot throughout.
notes: Once a food of hard times, when sweet potato stretched scarce rice, it is now a nostalgic late-night and breakfast dish.

recipes.name: Zhen zhu nai cha (bubble tea)
recipes.description: Iced black milk tea poured over chewy tapioca pearls soaked in brown sugar syrup. Taiwan's famous pearl milk tea, made at home with a wide straw.

ingredients.name: Strong black tea (Assam), from 4 tea bags or 2 tbsp leaves

steps.t: Brew the tea in 400 ml boiling water for 5 minutes, then strain or remove the bags. Cool and chill it; it needs to be cold so it doesn't melt all the ice.

Bring 1 litre of water to a rolling boil, add the pearls and stir until they float. Cook according to the packet, usually 5 minutes for quick-cook pearls or 20–30 minutes for standard ones, then turn off the heat, cover and leave for 10 minutes. They are ready when chewy all the way through with no hard white core.
Meanwhile make the syrup: dissolve the brown sugar in the 60 ml water in a small pan over medium heat, then simmer for 2–3 minutes until slightly thickened.
Drain the pearls, rinse them briefly under warm water and stir them into the warm syrup. Leave them to soak for 10 minutes; they absorb the sweetness and stay soft.

Spoon the pearls and syrup into the glasses, tilting and turning each glass so the syrup streaks the sides. Fill with ice, pour in the cold tea and the milk, stir and serve straight away with wide straws.

recipes.storage: Tapioca pearls harden as they cool and in the fridge, so drink within 2–3 hours of cooking them. The tea keeps 2 days in the fridge.
notes: Sweeten the tea itself with a little sugar if you like it sweeter; Taiwanese shops let you choose the sweetness level.

recipes.name: Kare raisu (Japanese chicken curry rice)
recipes.description: A thick, mild and slightly sweet curry of chicken, onion, carrot and potato, thickened with a homemade browned roux and served beside short-grain rice. Japan's favourite family dinner.

ingredients.name: Japanese curry powder (or a mild curry powder)
Potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 4 cm chunks

steps.t: Make the roux: melt the butter in the small saucepan over medium-low heat, add the flour and stir constantly for 8–10 minutes, until it turns light brown, like peanut butter, and smells nutty. A roux is flour cooked in fat; it thickens the sauce, and browning it gives Japanese curry its toasty depth. Stir in the curry powder for 30 seconds, then take it off the heat.
Heat the oil in the heavy pot over medium heat and fry the onions for 8–10 minutes, stirring often, until soft and golden. Add the garlic and ginger and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the chicken and cook for about 3 minutes, turning, until it is no longer pink on the outside. Add the carrots, potatoes, stock and grated apple and bring to the boil, skimming off any foam.
Cover and simmer over low heat for 15–20 minutes, until the potatoes and carrots are tender when pierced with a knife.

Turn off the heat. Ladle about 200 ml of the hot stock into the roux and whisk until smooth, then stir this paste back into the pot. Adding the roux off the heat, loosened first, stops it forming lumps.

Return to low heat and simmer for 5–10 minutes, stirring often so it doesn't catch, until the sauce is thick and glossy and coats the back of a spoon. Stir in the honey, soy sauce, ketchup and Worcestershire sauce, and add salt to taste. Check the chicken is cooked through.
Spoon rice onto one side of each plate and the curry onto the other, with pickles if you like. Japanese curry is famously even better the next day.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days. If freezing, pick out the potatoes first; they turn grainy.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently, stirring and adding a splash of water, until steaming hot throughout.
notes: Packet curry roux blocks are the everyday shortcut: use about 100 g in place of the butter, flour and curry powder, and skip the salt.
Beef chuck, simmered for an hour before adding the vegetables, is the other classic version.

recipes.name: Chicken katsu kare (katsu curry)
recipes.description: Crisp panko-crumbed chicken cutlets sliced and served on rice with a smooth, mild Japanese curry sauce poured alongside, plus shredded cabbage and pickles.

ingredients.name: Japanese curry powder (or a mild curry powder)

steps.t: Start the sauce: heat the oil in the saucepan over medium heat and fry the onion and carrot for 10 minutes, until soft and golden. Add the garlic and ginger for 30 seconds, pour in the stock and simmer, covered, for 15 minutes. Blend until smooth if you want the silky sauce of katsu-curry shops.

Meanwhile make a roux: melt the butter in the small pan over medium-low heat, stir in the flour and cook, stirring, for 5–8 minutes until light brown and nutty. Stir in the curry powder, then whisk in a ladleful of the hot stock until smooth and stir it all back into the saucepan. Simmer for 5 minutes, stirring, until thick, then season with the honey, soy sauce, ketchup and salt. Keep warm.
Slice each chicken breast in half horizontally to make 4 cutlets, then press or pound them to an even 1.5 cm thickness so they cook evenly. Season with salt and pepper.

Set out three plates: flour, beaten egg and panko. Dust each cutlet in flour and shake off the excess, dip it in the egg, then press it firmly into the panko on both sides so the crumbs stick. Rest for 5 minutes while the oil heats; the coating sets and stays on during frying.

Heat about 1.5 cm of oil in the frying pan to 170 °C. Fry the cutlets two at a time for 3–4 minutes per side, until deep golden and crisp and the centre reaches 74 °C. Drain on a wire rack rather than paper, which steams the underside soft.
Rest the katsu for 2 minutes, then cut each cutlet into 2 cm strips, keeping the shape together.

Mound rice on each plate, lay the sliced katsu against it and pour the curry sauce alongside rather than over the top, so the crust stays crisp. Add a pile of shredded cabbage and some pickles and serve.

recipes.storage: Keep the sauce and katsu separately in the fridge for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the sauce until steaming; re-crisp the katsu in a 200 °C oven for 8–10 minutes until piping hot throughout.
notes: Boneless thigh cutlets are juicier and more forgiving; fry them for 4–5 minutes per side.

recipes.name: Gyudon (beef and onion rice bowl)
recipes.description: Paper-thin beef and soft onion simmered briefly in a sweet soy and dashi broth, ladled with plenty of juices over hot rice and topped with red pickled ginger.
equipment: Small frying pan or shallow saucepan

ingredients.name: Beef ribeye or other well-marbled cut
ingredients.prep: sliced paper-thin, cut into 5–6 cm pieces

ingredients.name: Mirin and sake (use 1 tbsp less sugar with mirin)
Very fresh egg yolks or onsen eggs

steps.t: For paper-thin slices, freeze the beef for 30 minutes until firm, then slice it as thinly as you can across the grain; Asian grocers also sell it pre-sliced for sukiyaki or shabu-shabu. Cut it into 5–6 cm pieces.
Put the dashi, soy sauce and sugar (and the mirin and sake, if using) in the frying pan and bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves.
Add the onion and simmer for about 5 minutes, until soft, translucent and sweet.

Spread the beef over the onions, separating the slices with chopsticks. Simmer for 2–3 minutes, skimming off any grey foam, until the beef has just changed colour all over and soaked up some of the broth. Stir in the grated ginger. Don't let it simmer longer, or the thin beef turns tough and dry.
Fill two deep bowls with hot rice. Lift the beef and onion over it with chopsticks, then spoon over plenty of the broth so it soaks into the rice.
Top with red pickled ginger and spring onion and serve at once. For the classic rich finish, add a raw egg yolk or a soft onsen egg and break it into the hot beef.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Thinly sliced beef from the fatty short plate is used in gyudon chains; leaner cuts work but are less juicy.

recipes.name: Tori no karaage (Japanese fried chicken)
recipes.description: Juicy chunks of chicken thigh marinated in soy, ginger and garlic, coated in potato starch and fried twice until light, crackly and golden. Served with lemon, cabbage and rice.

steps.t: Mix the chicken with the soy sauce, ginger, garlic and sugar (and sake, if using) and leave to marinate for 30 minutes at room temperature or up to 6 hours in the fridge.
Mix the potato starch and flour on a plate. Potato starch gives a light, crackly crust; the little flour helps it brown and cling.
Pour the oil into the deep pan, no more than a third full, and heat it to 165 °C.

Lift the chicken out of the marinade, let the excess drip off and toss each piece in the starch mixture, shaking off the excess. Fry at 165 °C in batches of 5–6 pieces for about 3 minutes, until pale golden, then lift onto the rack. Leave them to rest for 4 minutes: the heat carries on cooking the centre gently while the oil comes back to temperature.

Heat the oil to 185 °C and fry the chicken again in batches for about 1 minute, until deep golden and very crisp. Check a large piece: the centre should reach 74 °C with no pink. This double-frying (nidoage) gives a crisp crust with juicy meat inside.
Drain on the rack for a minute and serve hot with lemon wedges to squeeze over, a pile of shredded cabbage, mayonnaise if you like and steamed rice.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Eat cold in a bento box, or re-crisp in a 200 °C oven or air fryer for 6–8 minutes until piping hot.

recipes.name: Okonomiyaki (Osaka-style savoury pancake)
recipes.description: A thick, fluffy pancake of finely chopped cabbage bound with a light dashi batter, topped with prawns, then finished with sweet-tangy okonomi sauce, mayonnaise and seaweed flakes.
equipment: Large frying pan with lid (or a hot plate)

ingredients.name: Thinly sliced pork belly, for the traditional topping
Aonori (green seaweed flakes) or a crumbled nori sheet

steps.t: Stir the ketchup, Worcestershire sauce, soy sauce and sugar together until the sugar dissolves. This is a quick okonomi sauce; bottled okonomiyaki sauce works too.

Whisk the flour and cold dashi into a smooth batter, adding the grated nagaimo if you have it; it makes the pancake lighter and fluffier. Leave to rest for 10 minutes. Meanwhile chop the cabbage finely, about 5 mm, and chop the prawns.

Just before cooking, add the eggs, cabbage, spring onions and pickled ginger to the batter and fold them in gently with a big spoon, lifting from the bottom to trap air. The mixture should look like mostly cabbage held together by batter; overmixing makes it dense.

Heat half the oil in the frying pan over medium heat. Spoon in half the mixture and shape it into a round about 18 cm across and 2 cm thick, without pressing it down. Scatter half the prawns over the top (or lay over pork belly slices, if using). Cover and cook for 4–5 minutes, until the underside is golden.

Slide two spatulas underneath and flip it over in one confident movement. Cook for 4–5 minutes, uncovered, then flip once more and cook for 1–2 minutes. Never press it flat. Push a skewer into the centre: it should come out hot with no raw batter, and the prawns should be pink.

Slide onto a plate, brush with the okonomi sauce, zigzag the mayonnaise across it and sprinkle with aonori, and bonito flakes if you have them; they wave in the rising heat. Keep it warm while you cook the second pancake, then cut into wedges and serve hot.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a covered frying pan over medium-low heat for 5–6 minutes until hot right through.
notes: 'Okonomi' means 'as you like': squid, pork belly, cheese or mochi are all common toppings.
Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki layers the ingredients over a thin crêpe and adds yakisoba noodles.

recipes.name: Yakisoba (Japanese stir-fried noodles)
recipes.description: Wheat noodles stir-fried with chicken, cabbage, carrot, onion and bean sprouts in a sticky, fruity Worcestershire-based sauce, finished with pickled ginger and seaweed flakes.

ingredients.name: Dried ramen or egg noodles (or 2 x 150 g packs fresh yakisoba noodles)
Thinly sliced pork belly, instead of the chicken (traditional)
Aonori (green seaweed flakes) or crumbled nori

steps.t: Cook the dried noodles for 1 minute less than the packet says, drain, rinse under cold water and drain well, then toss with a few drops of the oil so they don't clump. Fresh yakisoba noodles only need loosening: rinse them briefly under hot water and separate them with your fingers.
Stir the Worcestershire sauce, ketchup, oyster sauce, soy sauce and sugar together in a small bowl.

Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in the wok over high heat. Add the chicken and stir-fry for 3–4 minutes until browned and cooked through with no pink. Add the onion and carrot and stir-fry for 2 minutes, then the cabbage for another 2 minutes, until it wilts but still has some crunch.
Push everything to the side, add the remaining oil and the noodles and spread them out. Leave them for 1 minute so they pick up a little colour, then toss them with the vegetables.

Add the bean sprouts and pour the sauce over. Toss with tongs or chopsticks for 1–2 minutes, until the noodles are evenly coated and the sauce has turned sticky and slightly caramelised in the hot wok.
Divide between plates, top with red pickled ginger and aonori and serve hot, the way it is sold at Japanese summer festivals.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Tamagoyaki (Japanese rolled omelette)
recipes.description: A lightly sweet omelette built up in thin layers and rolled into a neat, tender log, then sliced. A breakfast and bento staple; Kansai cooks make a savoury dashi version.
equipment: Rectangular tamagoyaki pan (or a 20 cm non-stick frying pan)

steps.t: Beat the eggs gently with chopsticks, cutting through the whites rather than whisking, so you don't create foam. Stir in the sugar, soy sauce, water and salt (and mirin, if using) until the sugar dissolves. For a very smooth omelette, pour it through a sieve.

Heat the pan over medium-low heat. Fold a piece of kitchen paper, dip it in the oil and wipe a thin film over the pan; keep the paper for re-oiling between layers. The pan is ready when a drop of egg sizzles gently, not fiercely.

Pour in about a quarter of the egg and tilt the pan to cover the base. Pop any large bubbles. When the bottom has set but the top is still slightly wet, after 30–60 seconds, roll the egg up from the far end towards you in 3–4 folds, using chopsticks or a thin spatula.

Push the roll back to the far end of the pan and wipe the empty part with the oiled paper. Pour in another quarter of the egg and lift the roll so the raw egg runs underneath it. When it is almost set, roll the omelette back towards you, wrapping the new layer around it. Repeat with the remaining egg; sugar makes the egg brown quickly, so lower the heat if it colours too much.
Turn the omelette out onto a bamboo mat or a sheet of baking paper, roll it up tightly to square off the shape and leave for 5 minutes. It firms up and finishes cooking in its own heat.
Slice into 2 cm pieces and serve warm or at room temperature, with grated daikon and a drop of soy sauce, as part of a breakfast with rice and miso soup, or packed in a bento box.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate and eat within 2 days; it is often eaten cold in bento boxes.
notes: Dashimaki tamago, the Kansai style, uses 4 tablespoons of dashi instead of the water and only a teaspoon of sugar; it is softer and juicier but harder to roll.

recipes.name: Salmon teriyaki (sake no teriyaki)
recipes.description: Salmon fillets pan-fried with a crisp skin, then glazed in a glossy soy and sugar sauce until sticky. A quick weeknight dinner with rice and greens.

ingredients.name: Mirin and sake (replace the water and half the sugar)

steps.t: Pat the salmon dry, sprinkle both sides with the salt and leave for 10 minutes. The salt draws out moisture that carries any fishy smell; pat the fillets dry again, then dust them lightly with flour, which helps the glaze cling.
Stir the soy sauce, sugar and water together until the sugar dissolves. If using mirin and sake, use them in place of the water and halve the sugar.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat. Lay the salmon in skin side down and cook without moving it for 3–4 minutes, until the skin is crisp and the flesh has turned opaque about two-thirds of the way up the sides.
Turn the fillets and cook for 1–2 minutes. Wipe the fat out of the pan with kitchen paper so the sauce can reduce to a glaze rather than mixing with oil.
Pour in the sauce and let it bubble, spooning it over the salmon, for 1–2 minutes until thick and glossy. The fish is done when it flakes easily and is opaque in the centre (63 °C).
Serve straight away with rice and steamed greens, spooning over the last of the glaze, and scatter with spring onion if you like.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Eat leftovers cold, flaked over rice, or warm gently in a covered pan; overheating dries the fish.

recipes.name: Nikujaga (beef and potato simmer)
recipes.description: Thinly sliced beef, potatoes, onion and carrot gently simmered in sweet soy and dashi until the potatoes are tender and full of flavour. Japan's archetypal 'mother's cooking'.
equipment: Drop lid (otoshibuta) or a circle of baking paper

ingredients.name: Floury or all-purpose potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 4 cm chunks

steps.t: Cut the potatoes into chunks and, if you like, trim the sharp edges with a peeler so they don't crumble as they simmer. Soak them in water for 5 minutes, then drain. Cut the onions into wedges and the carrot into chunks.

Heat the oil in the heavy pot over medium-high heat. Fry the beef for 1–2 minutes until it changes colour, then add the onions and stir for 2 minutes. Add the potatoes and carrot (and the shirataki, if using) and turn them in the oil for 2 minutes.
Pour in the dashi and bring to the boil. Skim off the grey foam that rises, which would cloud the broth.

Add the sugar and simmer for 3 minutes before adding the soy sauce (and mirin and sake, if using). Japanese cooks add sugar first because it takes longer to penetrate the vegetables; soy sauce added too early would firm them up and stop the sweetness soaking in.

Lay a drop lid or a circle of baking paper with a small hole in the centre directly on the surface. This keeps everything submerged in the shallow liquid and stops the potatoes tumbling and breaking. Simmer over medium-low heat for 15–20 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the liquid has reduced by about half.
Add the peas and cook for 2 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave the pot covered for 10–15 minutes: as it cools, the potatoes soak up the broth and take on more flavour.
Reheat gently and serve in bowls with a little of the cooking liquid, alongside rice and miso soup.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Nikujaga tastes even better the next day.
