recipes.name: Chawanmushi (savoury steamed egg custard)
recipes.description: A silky, barely set custard of egg and dashi steamed in cups over chicken, prawn and mushroom. Served hot as a starter, eaten with a spoon.
equipment: Steamer or large pot with a rack and lid

steps.t: Make sure the dashi has cooled to room temperature; hot dashi starts cooking the egg and the custard turns grainy. Beat the eggs gently with chopsticks so they don't foam, then stir in the dashi, soy sauce and salt (and mirin, if using). Strain twice through the fine sieve.
Toss the chicken with a few drops of soy sauce. Divide the chicken, prawns, mushrooms and kamaboko (if using) between the four cups.
Pour the egg mixture gently over the fillings, to about 1 cm below the rim. Pop any bubbles on the surface with a toothpick, then cover each cup with a lid or a square of foil.

Bring the water in the steamer to the boil, put the cups on the rack and cover. Turn the heat to low so the water only just simmers, and wedge a chopstick under the lid to let a little steam escape. Gentle heat (about 85–90 °C) is the secret: fierce steam makes the custard puff up and fill with holes.

Steam for 12–15 minutes. Test by pushing a skewer into the centre of one cup: if clear broth wells up rather than cloudy liquid egg, it is done. The custard should wobble like soft tofu, and the chicken should be cooked through.
Top with a mitsuba or parsley leaf and serve straight away, with spoons, as a starter or part of a Japanese meal.

recipes.storage: Best eaten freshly steamed. Refrigerate leftovers and eat within 1 day; in summer it is also eaten chilled.
recipes.reheating: Steam gently for 5 minutes until hot through.
notes: The ratio is 1 part egg to 3 parts dashi by volume; keep to it and the custard always sets softly.

recipes.name: Agedashi dofu (fried tofu in dashi broth)
recipes.description: Cubes of tofu dusted in potato starch and fried until delicately crisp, then served in a warm soy and kelp dashi broth with grated daikon, ginger and spring onion.

ingredients.name: Kombu dashi (kelp stock) or light vegetable stock

steps.t: Wrap the tofu in kitchen paper, set a plate on top and leave for 15–20 minutes to press out excess water; drier tofu fries crisper and spits less. Cut it into 8 cubes and pat them dry.
Put the dashi, soy sauce and sugar (or mirin) in the small saucepan and bring just to a simmer. Keep it warm over the lowest heat.
Grate the daikon and squeeze it gently to remove some liquid. Grate the ginger and slice the spring onion.
Heat the oil in the deep pan, no more than a third full, to 175 °C. Just before frying, roll each tofu cube in the starch to coat it thinly on all sides; coating too early turns the starch gummy.
Fry 3–4 cubes at a time at 175 °C for 3–4 minutes, turning gently, until pale golden and crisp. Lift onto the wire rack to drain while you fry the rest.

Put two cubes in each shallow bowl and pour the hot broth around them. Top with a mound of daikon, a little ginger and the spring onion and serve immediately: the crust turns silky where it meets the broth while the top stays crisp.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately; the crust softens and it doesn't keep well.
notes: For kombu dashi, soak a 10 cm piece of kombu (kelp) in 300 ml water for 30 minutes, then heat until just below boiling and lift out the kombu. Bonito dashi is the other classic choice.
Bonito flakes are a common topping; leave them off to keep the dish vegan.

recipes.name: Zaru soba (chilled soba with dipping sauce)
recipes.description: Buckwheat noodles boiled, rinsed and chilled in iced water, served on a bamboo tray with nori and a cold dashi and soy dipping sauce. A refreshing summer lunch.

ingredients.name: Nori sheet
ingredients.prep: cut into thin strips with scissors

steps.t: Make the dipping sauce: bring the dashi, soy sauce and sugar (or mirin) to a simmer in the small saucepan, stirring until the sugar dissolves, then cool it quickly by setting the pan in iced water. Chill until needed; it can be made days ahead.
Slice the spring onions very thinly and cut the nori into fine strips. Set out the wasabi, if using.

Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil; soba releases a lot of starch and needs plenty of water. Scatter in the noodles and stir gently so they don't stick. When the water foams up towards the rim, add a splash of cold water to calm it. Cook according to the packet, usually 4–5 minutes, until tender with a slight firmness in the centre.

Drain the soba and rinse it under cold running water, rubbing the noodles gently between your hands to wash off the surface starch; this keeps them clean-tasting and not slimy. Plunge them into iced water for 30 seconds to firm them up, then drain very well.
Pile the noodles on bamboo trays or plates and scatter the nori over the top. Pour the chilled sauce into small cups.

To eat, stir spring onion and a little wasabi into the sauce, then pick up a mouthful of noodles, dip them about a third of the way into the sauce and slurp. At soba shops the noodle cooking water (sobayu) is poured into the leftover sauce at the end and drunk like a soup.

recipes.storage: Cook soba just before eating; it turns soft and clumps once cooked. The dipping sauce keeps 1 week in the fridge.
notes: Most soba contains some wheat flour; 100% buckwheat (juwari) soba is gluten-free but more fragile.

recipes.name: Dorayaki (red bean pancakes)
recipes.description: Two soft, honey-sweet pancakes, evenly golden, sandwiched around a thick layer of sweet red bean paste. A classic Japanese teatime sweet.

ingredients.name: Sweet red bean paste (anko), chunky or smooth

steps.t: Whisk the eggs, sugar and honey together for 2–3 minutes, until pale, thick and the sugar has dissolved. The air whisked in now makes the pancakes light.

Dissolve the bicarbonate of soda in 1 tablespoon of the water and whisk it in. Sift in the flour and fold it in gently until just smooth. Cover and rest for 15 minutes, then stir in more of the remaining water a little at a time until the batter falls from the whisk in a thick ribbon, like a thick pancake batter.

Heat the frying pan over medium-low heat. Wipe it with a piece of kitchen paper dipped in the oil, then wipe again with a clean piece so only a trace of oil remains; this gives the even, spotless golden colour dorayaki are known for.

Pour about 1½ tablespoons of batter from a little height into the centre of the pan so it spreads into a neat 8 cm circle. Cook for 1½–2 minutes, until bubbles appear on the surface and the edges look dry, then flip and cook for 30–45 seconds more. Transfer to a plate and cover with the damp tea towel so the pancakes stay soft. Repeat to make 12.

Pair the pancakes by size. Spread about 2 heaped tablespoons of red bean paste on the pale side of one, mounding it slightly in the middle, and top with its partner, golden side up. Press the edges together gently so the filling is sealed in.
Wrap each dorayaki in cling film and leave for 15 minutes so the shape sets and the pancakes soften around the filling. Serve at room temperature, with green tea.

recipes.storage: Wrap individually and keep at room temperature for 1 day or in the fridge for up to 3 days; bring back to room temperature before eating.
notes: Ready-made anko is sold in tins and pouches at Asian grocers; homemade red bean paste is less sweet.

recipes.name: Gyoza (Japanese pan-fried dumplings)
recipes.description: Thin-skinned dumplings filled with juicy chicken, cabbage and garlic chives, fried until crisp underneath, steamed until tender on top, and dipped in soy, vinegar and chilli oil.
equipment: Large non-stick frying pan with a lid

steps.t: Toss the chopped cabbage with the salt and leave for 10 minutes, then squeeze it hard in your hands or a cloth to remove as much water as possible.

Put the chicken, garlic, ginger, soy sauce, sesame oil, starch and white pepper in a bowl and knead with your hand for 1–2 minutes, until the mixture turns pale and sticky; this binds the filling so it stays juicy. Mix in the cabbage and chives.

Hold a wrapper in one palm and put a heaped teaspoon of filling in the centre. Wet half the edge with a fingertip dipped in water, fold the wrapper over and make 5–6 small pleats along the front edge, pressing each against the flat back edge. You end up with a crescent that sits on a flat base. Set the gyoza on a floured tray and keep them covered while you fill the rest.
Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in the frying pan over medium heat. Arrange the gyoza flat side down in tight rows or a circle, just touching. Fry for 2–3 minutes, until the bases are golden.

Pour in the 100 ml water, standing back because it spits, and cover immediately. Steam for 5–6 minutes, until the water has almost evaporated, the wrappers look translucent and the filling is cooked through (74 °C, no pink).

Take off the lid and drizzle the remaining oil and the sesame oil around the edges. Fry for 1–2 minutes more until the bases are crisp again and the gyoza slide when you shake the pan. Put a plate over the pan and turn it over so the crisp bases face up.
Mix the soy sauce and vinegar, add chilli oil to taste, and serve the gyoza hot with the dipping sauce, as a starter, with ramen or as part of a meal with rice.

recipes.storage: Freeze uncooked gyoza on the floured tray until hard, then bag them for up to 1 month; cook from frozen, steaming 2 minutes longer. Refrigerate cooked leftovers and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-fry in a little oil in a covered pan until crisp and steaming hot.
notes: Pork is the usual filling in Japan; chicken thigh mince keeps it juicy and halal-friendly.
For crisp lacy 'wings' (hanetsuki), stir 1 teaspoon of flour into the steaming water.

recipes.name: Kimchi jjigae (kimchi stew with tuna)
recipes.description: Sour, well-fermented kimchi fried in sesame oil, then simmered into a spicy, deeply savoury stew with canned tuna and soft tofu. Korea's everyday comfort food, eaten bubbling hot with rice.
equipment: Medium saucepan or Korean earthenware pot (ttukbaegi)

ingredients.name: Well-fermented (sour) cabbage kimchi, plus 4 tbsp of its juice

steps.t: Cut the kimchi into bite-sized pieces with scissors, keeping its juice. Slice the onion, cut the tofu into thick squares and slice the spring onions and chilli. Old, sour kimchi makes the best jjigae; fresh kimchi tastes flat here.

Heat the sesame oil in the pot over medium heat. Add the kimchi and onion and fry, stirring, for 4–5 minutes, until the kimchi is soft, translucent and lightly caramelised at the edges. Frying mellows the sourness and builds the stew's flavour.
Add the garlic, gochugaru and gochujang and stir for 1 minute until the paste coats the kimchi and smells toasty.
Pour in the water and the kimchi juice and bring to the boil. Simmer over medium heat for 10 minutes, until the broth is red and full-flavoured and the kimchi is tender.
Add the tuna in large flakes and the tofu and simmer for 5 minutes more. Taste: add the soy sauce, and the sugar if the kimchi is very sour, plus a little salt if needed.
Scatter over the spring onions and chilli, simmer for 1 minute and bring the pot to the table bubbling. Eat with bowls of steamed rice.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Tuna canned in oil gives a richer stew; drain off most of the oil first.
For a vegetarian version, leave out the tuna and use kelp-shiitake stock; most kimchi contains fish sauce or salted shrimp, so check the label.

recipes.name: Sundubu jjigae (soft tofu stew with seafood)
recipes.description: Silky, custard-soft tofu in a fiery red broth with clams and prawns, finished with an egg cracked into the bubbling pot.
equipment: Small saucepan or two Korean earthenware pots (ttukbaegi)

steps.t: Soak the clams in salted water (1 teaspoon of salt per 500 ml) for 30 minutes so they spit out sand, then scrub them. Discard any that are cracked or that stay open when tapped.

Make the chilli oil base: put the oil, sesame oil, garlic, onion and half the spring onion in the pot over low heat and cook for 2 minutes until soft and fragrant. Turn off the heat, add the gochugaru and stir for 30 seconds; the remaining heat turns the oil red without burning the chilli.
Return to medium heat, pour in the stock, soy sauce and fish sauce and bring to the boil.
Add the clams and prawns and cook for 2–3 minutes, until the clams open and the prawns turn pink. Discard any clams that stay shut.
Squeeze or spoon the tofu into the pot in large pieces and simmer gently for 3–4 minutes. Don't stir hard: the tofu should stay in soft, creamy curds. Taste and add salt if needed.

Crack the eggs into the middle, scatter over the rest of the spring onion and cook for 1–2 minutes, until the whites are set. Serve bubbling in the pot with steamed rice, and stir the egg into the stew as you eat.

recipes.storage: Best eaten freshly made. Refrigerate leftovers promptly and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Sundubu tofu is softer than silken tofu sold in blocks and comes in tubes at Korean grocers; the softest silken tofu is the nearest substitute.

recipes.name: Doenjang jjigae (soybean paste stew)
recipes.description: A hearty, earthy stew of fermented soybean paste with potato, courgette, mushrooms, onion and tofu, simmered in kelp and shiitake stock. Salty, savoury and made for rice.
equipment: Medium saucepan or Korean earthenware pot (ttukbaegi)

ingredients.name: Kelp and shiitake stock (or vegetable stock)

steps.t: Soak the dried shiitake in the stock for 20 minutes (a 10 cm piece of kelp can soak with them). Bring to the boil, simmer for 5 minutes, then lift out the kelp, slice the shiitake and return them to the pot.
Cut the potato, onion, courgette and tofu and slice the chillies and spring onion while the stock simmers.
Put the doenjang in a small sieve, lower it into the stock and press it through with a spoon so it dissolves completely with no lumps.
Add the potato, bring back to the boil and simmer for 7–8 minutes, until it is almost tender. Potatoes go in first because they take longest.
Add the onion, courgette, mushrooms, garlic and gochugaru and simmer for 5 minutes, until the courgette is just tender.

Add the tofu and chillies and simmer for 3 minutes more. Taste: doenjang jjigae should be salty and savoury, and a little water softens it if it is too strong. Scatter with spring onion and serve bubbling with rice and side dishes.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Many households use anchovy-kelp stock or add a few clams or strips of beef; this version keeps it plant-based.
Korean doenjang is chunkier and funkier than Japanese miso; miso works but gives a milder, sweeter stew.

recipes.name: Sukju namul (seasoned bean sprouts)
recipes.description: Bean sprouts blanched until just tender and still crunchy, then tossed with garlic, spring onion, sesame oil and toasted sesame seeds. A staple banchan and bibimbap topping.

ingredients.name: Soy sauce (Korean soup soy sauce if you have it)

steps.t: Rinse the bean sprouts in a bowl of cold water and pick out any loose green husks or brown tails.
Bring a saucepan of water to the boil with the half teaspoon of salt. Add the sprouts and blanch for 1–2 minutes, just until they lose their raw taste but still snap when bitten.
Drain them and rinse under cold water to stop the cooking, then shake well and squeeze gently to remove excess water so the seasoning doesn't get diluted.

Put the sprouts in the bowl with the garlic, spring onion, salt, soy sauce, sesame oil and sesame seeds (and gochugaru, if using). Toss and gently massage with your fingertips so the seasoning coats every sprout.
Taste, adjust the salt and serve at room temperature or chilled as one of several banchan with rice, or pile onto bibimbap.

recipes.storage: Keep in a covered container in the fridge for up to 2 days.
notes: Kongnamul muchim is the same dish made with soybean sprouts: boil them with the lid on for 5 minutes, without lifting it, so they don't taste beany.

recipes.name: Dakgalbi (spicy stir-fried chicken)
recipes.description: Chicken marinated in a sweet, fiery gochujang sauce and stir-fried at the table with cabbage, sweet potato, onion and spring onions until sticky. Finish the pan with fried rice.
equipment: Very large frying pan, cast-iron skillet or tabletop griddle

ingredients.name: Sweet potato
ingredients.prep: peeled, halved and sliced 5 mm thick

ingredients.name: Cooked short-grain rice, for the fried-rice finish
Nori sheet, crumbled, for the fried rice

steps.t: Mix all the marinade ingredients in a bowl, add the chicken and turn it until well coated. Marinate for at least 30 minutes, or overnight in the fridge for the best flavour.
Cut the cabbage, slice the sweet potato thinly so it cooks in the same time as the chicken, and cut the onion and spring onions.
Heat the oil in the large pan over medium-high heat. Spread the cabbage, sweet potato and onion over the base and put the chicken and all its marinade on top.

Cook for about 5 minutes without stirring: the cabbage releases its juices and steams the chicken. Then start turning everything over and over with two spatulas, the way Chuncheon restaurants do at the table, and keep stir-frying for 10–12 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through (no pink, 74 °C), the sweet potato is tender and the sauce is thick and clinging. Lower the heat if the sauce starts to catch.
Add the spring onions and perilla leaves (if using) and stir for 1 minute until just wilted.

Bring the pan to the table and serve with lettuce leaves for wrapping and rice on the side. For the classic finish, when about a quarter is left, add the cooked rice, crumbled nori and a drizzle of sesame oil, chop everything together with the spatula and press it flat to fry until crisp underneath.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Chuncheon restaurants add chewy rice cakes (tteok) with the vegetables; add 200 g if you can find them.

recipes.name: Gimbap (Korean seaweed rice rolls)
recipes.description: Sesame-seasoned rice and colourful fillings of seasoned beef, egg, spinach, carrot and yellow pickled radish rolled in seaweed and sliced into rounds. Korea's favourite picnic food.

ingredients.name: Eggs
ingredients.prep: beaten with a pinch of salt

steps.t: Gently mix the warm rice with the tablespoon of sesame oil and the salt using a spatula, cutting rather than mashing so the grains stay whole. Spread it out to cool to room temperature; hot rice makes the seaweed shrink and tear.
Fry the beef in ½ tablespoon of the oil over medium-high heat with the soy sauce, sugar and garlic, breaking it up, for 4–5 minutes until cooked through and the pan is dry. Cool.

Wipe the pan, add a little oil and pour in the eggs over low heat to make a thin omelette. Cook for 2–3 minutes until set, flip for 30 seconds, then cool and cut into 1 cm strips. In the same pan, stir-fry the carrots with a pinch of salt for 1–2 minutes until just softened.

Blanch the spinach in boiling water for 30 seconds, rinse it in cold water and squeeze it dry, then season with a pinch of salt and a few drops of sesame oil. Pat the pickled radish strips dry. Wet fillings make the roll soggy and loosen it.

Lay a nori sheet shiny side down on the bamboo mat. With damp fingers, spread a quarter of the rice thinly and evenly over it, leaving a 3 cm strip bare at the far edge. Arrange a quarter of each filling in neat rows across the third nearest you.

Lift the edge of the mat and roll it over the fillings, tucking them in tightly, then keep rolling forward, pressing firmly, until you reach the bare strip. Press a few grains of rice onto it to seal the roll. Repeat to make 4 rolls.

Brush the rolls with sesame oil and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Slice each into 1.5 cm rounds with a very sharp knife, wiping the blade with a damp cloth between cuts so it doesn't drag. Serve at room temperature.

recipes.storage: Eat the same day, kept cool; refrigerating hardens the rice. Leftover slices can be dipped in beaten egg and pan-fried.
notes: Danmuji is sold in long strips at Korean grocers, often in a gimbap kit with burdock root.
Canned tuna mixed with mayonnaise, or crab sticks, are popular alternatives to the beef.

recipes.name: Haemul pajeon (seafood and spring onion pancake)
recipes.description: Whole spring onions bound in a thin, crisp batter with squid and prawns, fried until lacy and golden and cut into squares to dip in a tangy soy sauce. A rainy-day favourite.

ingredients.name: Spring onions (about 2 bunches)
ingredients.prep: trimmed to 20 cm lengths, thick ends halved

ingredients.name: Squid
ingredients.prep: cleaned and cut into thin rings

ingredients.name: Egg, beaten, to drizzle on top

steps.t: Whisk the flour, rice flour, salt, egg and ice-cold water into a thin batter; a few small lumps are fine. Ice-cold water and minimal mixing keep the gluten relaxed, so the pancake turns crisp rather than chewy. Keep the batter in the fridge until needed.
Trim the spring onions to fit the pan and halve any thick white ends lengthwise. Pat the squid and prawns dry. Stir the dipping sauce ingredients together.

Heat 2 tablespoons of the oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat. Lay half the spring onions in the pan side by side in a single layer, then spoon over enough batter to just bind them. Scatter half the squid, prawns and chilli on top, drizzle over a little more batter to fill the gaps and finish with half the beaten egg.

Cook for 4–5 minutes, until the underside is golden and crisp and the edges look lacy. Slide it onto a plate, invert the pan over it and flip it back in. Add another tablespoon of oil around the edge and cook for 4 minutes more, pressing down now and then with the spatula, until crisp and the seafood is cooked through (prawns pink, squid opaque).
Flip it once more for a final minute to re-crisp the top, then slide onto a board. Cook the second pancake the same way.
Cut into squares and serve hot with the dipping sauce.

recipes.storage: Best eaten hot. Refrigerate leftovers and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes per side until hot through.
notes: Leave out the seafood for plain pajeon, or add chopped kimchi to the batter for kimchijeon.

recipes.name: Yangnyeom chikin (Korean fried chicken)
recipes.description: Chicken wings in a thin starch batter, double-fried until glassy and crisp, then tossed in a sticky sweet and spicy gochujang glaze with peanuts and sesame seeds.
equipment: Wide frying pan or wok for the glaze

steps.t: Pat the wings very dry and season them with the salt, pepper and garlic powder. Leave for 15 minutes.

Whisk the starch, flour, baking powder and cold water into a thin batter with the consistency of single cream. The mostly-starch batter fries into the thin, crackly shell Korean fried chicken is known for.
Heat the oil in the deep pan, no more than a third full, to 170 °C.

Dip the wings in the batter, letting the excess drip off, and fry in batches for 8–10 minutes, turning occasionally, until light golden and cooked through to the bone (74 °C). Lift onto the rack and rest for 5 minutes.

Heat the oil to 185 °C and fry all the wings again in batches for 3–4 minutes, until deep golden and glassy-crisp. The second fry drives out the last moisture, so the crust stays crisp even under the glaze.

For the glaze, warm the tablespoon of oil and the garlic in the wide pan over low heat for 1 minute, then add the gochujang, ketchup, syrup, sugar, soy sauce and water. Simmer for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until thick, glossy and bubbling.

Take the pan off the heat, add the hot wings and toss quickly until evenly coated. Pile onto a platter, scatter with peanuts and sesame seeds and serve straight away with cubes of pickled radish and something cold to drink.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat on a rack in a 200 °C oven for 10 minutes until piping hot; the glaze softens the crust a little.
notes: Order 'banban' (half and half) style by tossing only half the wings in the glaze and serving the rest plain with salt.

recipes.name: Galbi-jjim (braised beef short ribs)
recipes.description: Beef short ribs braised slowly in a sweet soy sauce with Asian pear, garlic and sesame, with radish, carrot, shiitake and jujubes, until the meat falls from the bone. A centrepiece for Chuseok and Lunar New Year.

ingredients.name: Beef short ribs, bone-in, cut into 5 cm pieces

steps.t: Soak the ribs in cold water for 1 hour, changing the water once or twice, to draw out the blood. Trim off thick pieces of fat and cut a few slashes into the meat so the sauce can penetrate.
Put the ribs in the pot, cover with fresh water and boil for 5–7 minutes, until grey foam rises. Drain, rinse each rib and wash the pot. Parboiling gives a cleaner, less greasy sauce.

Blend or grate the pear, onion, garlic and ginger to a purée and mix it with the soy sauce, brown sugar, sesame oil and black pepper (and the rice wine, if using). Pear sweetens the sauce and its enzymes help tenderise the meat.
Return the ribs to the pot with the sauce and the 500 ml water. Bring to the boil, cover and simmer over low heat for 1 hour, turning the ribs once or twice.
Meanwhile cut the radish and carrots into chunks and trim the sharp edges so they don't break up in the long braise. Soak the shiitake in warm water for 20 minutes and halve them.
Add the radish, carrots, shiitake and jujubes, cover and simmer for 30–40 minutes more, until the meat is tender enough to pull from the bone and the radish is translucent.

Skim the fat from the surface with a spoon (or chill the braise overnight and lift off the solid fat). Uncover and simmer for about 10 minutes, spooning the sauce over, until it has reduced to a glossy glaze that coats the ribs.
Pile the ribs and vegetables onto a platter, spoon over the sauce and scatter with spring onions and pine nuts. Serve with steamed rice and banchan.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days in the fridge and freezes well; it tastes better the next day.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Peeled chestnuts and ginkgo nuts are traditional additions with the vegetables.
In a pressure cooker, cook the parboiled ribs in the sauce for 25 minutes at high pressure, then add the vegetables and simmer uncovered until tender.

recipes.name: Samgyetang (ginseng chicken soup)
recipes.description: A whole young chicken stuffed with sticky rice, garlic, jujube and ginseng, simmered until the meat falls from the bone in a milky, restorative broth. Seasoned at the table with salt and pepper.

ingredients.name: Poussins or Cornish hens (2, about 450 g each)
Fresh ginseng (2 small roots), or dried ginseng

steps.t: Soak the glutinous rice in cold water for 1 hour, then drain. Rinse the birds inside and out, pull away any lumps of fat around the cavity, trim off the wing tips and pat dry.
Stuff each cavity with half the rice, 2 garlic cloves, 1 jujube and 1 ginseng root (and pine nuts, if using). Don't pack it tightly: the rice swells as it cooks.
Close the cavity so the stuffing stays in: cut a small slit in the loose skin of one thigh and tuck the other leg through it to cross the legs, or tie them with string.
Put the birds in the pot with the remaining garlic and jujubes and the water, which should just cover them. Bring to the boil over high heat and skim off the foam as it rises.

Lower the heat, cover and simmer gently for 60–70 minutes, until the meat is very tender, a leg moves loosely in its joint and the rice inside is soft. The thickest part of the thigh should reach 74 °C. The broth turns pale and milky.

Lift each bird into a large bowl and ladle the hot broth around it. Scatter with spring onion and serve with small dishes of salt and pepper for seasoning at the table, and kimchi on the side. Break the bird open as you eat so the sticky rice thickens the broth.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Koreans eat samgyetang on the three hottest days of summer (boknal), fighting heat with heat.
Dried ginseng and jujubes are sold together as samgyetang packs in Korean grocers.

recipes.name: Hotteok (sweet filled pancakes)
recipes.description: Soft, chewy yeasted pancakes stuffed with brown sugar, cinnamon and peanuts, pressed flat and fried until crisp, so the filling melts into a hot syrup. A winter street snack.

steps.t: Stir the sugar and yeast into the lukewarm water and leave for 5 minutes, until foamy; this shows the yeast is alive. Mix the flour, glutinous rice flour and salt in a bowl, add the yeast water and the tablespoon of oil and beat with a spoon for 2 minutes into a soft, sticky dough. It is much wetter than bread dough.
Cover and leave somewhere warm for about 1 hour, until doubled and bubbly. Punch it down, cover and rest for 15 minutes more.
Mix the brown sugar, cinnamon and chopped nuts for the filling.

Oil your hands, as the dough is sticky. Take an eighth of the dough, flatten it into a 10 cm disc in your palm and put a heaped tablespoon of filling in the centre. Pull the edges up over the filling and pinch them together tightly, like a dumpling. Set it seam side down on an oiled plate and repeat.

Heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the frying pan over medium heat. Add 2–3 balls seam side down and fry for 1 minute until golden. Turn them, then press each one flat with an oiled spatula into a 12 cm round about 1 cm thick. Fry for 1–2 minutes, then turn again, lower the heat to medium-low and cover for 1–2 minutes so the sugar inside melts into syrup.

When both sides are golden and crisp, lift them out and cook the rest, adding more oil as needed. Serve warm, folded in half in a paper cup the way Seoul stalls do, and bite carefully: the syrup inside is very hot.

recipes.storage: Best eaten warm. Keep cooled hotteok airtight for 1 day, or freeze for 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a dry frying pan over low heat for 2–3 minutes per side until the filling is runny again.
notes: Seed hotteok, popular in Busan, is split open and stuffed with mixed sunflower and pumpkin seeds.

recipes.name: Patbingsu (red bean shaved ice)
recipes.description: Fluffy, snow-like shaved frozen milk piled high and topped with sweet red beans and a drizzle of condensed milk. Korea's favourite summer dessert, made for sharing.
equipment: Shallow freezer container or ice-cube trays

ingredients.name: Sweetened condensed milk, for the milk ice

steps.t: At least 4 hours ahead, or the day before, whisk the milk with 2 tablespoons of condensed milk until smooth. Pour it into a shallow container or ice-cube trays and freeze until completely solid. Frozen sweetened milk shaves into softer, creamier flakes than plain ice.
Chill two serving bowls in the freezer for 15 minutes so the shaved ice doesn't melt on contact.

Let the frozen milk stand for 2–3 minutes to soften very slightly. Shave it with an ice shaver, or break it into cubes and pulse in a powerful blender or food processor in short bursts until it looks like fluffy snow. Without either, scrape it with a fork for a granita-like texture.
Pile the milk snow into a high mound in each chilled bowl.
Spoon the red beans over the top, drizzle with the condensed milk and add fresh fruit if you like. Chewy rice-cake cubes and roasted soybean powder are the classic extras.
Serve immediately with long spoons, mixing the toppings into the ice as you eat.

recipes.storage: Serve as soon as it is shaved; it melts within minutes. Frozen milk cubes keep 1 month in the freezer.

recipes.name: Buuz (Mongolian steamed meat dumplings)
recipes.description: Plump steamed dumplings of minced lamb, onion and garlic, pleated around the top with a small opening so the juices stay inside. Made by the hundred for the Lunar New Year, Tsagaan Sar.
equipment: Steamer (bamboo or metal) over a pot

ingredients.name: Lamb or mutton mince, with some fat (or fatty beef mince)

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt, add the water gradually and knead for 8–10 minutes into a smooth, fairly firm dough. It should be a little firmer than Chinese dumpling dough so the buuz hold their upright shape while steaming. Cover and rest for 30 minutes.

Put the mince, onion, garlic, salt and pepper (and caraway, if using) in a bowl. Work in the cold water a little at a time with your hand, squeezing and mixing for about 2 minutes, until the filling is sticky and has absorbed all the water. This water turns into the juice inside each dumpling.
Roll the dough into a log and cut it into 24 pieces of about 25 g. Roll each into a 9–10 cm round, making the edges thinner than the centre so the top of the dumpling isn't doughy.

Hold a wrapper in your palm and put a heaped tablespoon of filling in the middle. With the other hand, pinch a small pleat at the edge, then keep making pleats all the way around, turning the dumpling as you go, so the wrapper gathers up around the filling. Leave a small opening at the top, the classic buuz shape that lets steam escape. Set them on a floured tray.

Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil. Brush the steamer with oil and arrange the buuz 2 cm apart. Steam over high heat for 15–20 minutes, until the dough is set, glossy and no longer sticky, and the filling is cooked through, with clear juices bubbling at the opening.
Serve hot, in batches straight from the steamer, with a cabbage or carrot salad and salty milk tea. Mongolians bite a small hole in the side first and sip out the hot juice before eating the rest.

recipes.storage: Freeze uncooked buuz on a floured tray, then bag them, for up to 2 months; steam from frozen for 25 minutes. Refrigerate cooked leftovers and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Steam for 8–10 minutes until piping hot throughout.
notes: Mutton with plenty of fat is traditional; very lean mince gives dry buuz.

recipes.name: Tsuivan (Mongolian noodles with lamb and vegetables)
recipes.description: Thin sheets of homemade dough steamed on top of fried lamb and vegetables, then cut into noodles and tossed back into the pan so they soak up the meat juices.
equipment: Wide heavy pot or deep frying pan with a tight lid

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt with the water and knead for 5 minutes into a smooth, firm dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Divide the dough into 3 pieces and roll each into a thin sheet, about 2 mm thick and roughly the width of your pan. Brush the sheets with oil so they don't stick together later.
Heat the 2 tablespoons of oil in the wide pot over high heat. Add the lamb and fry for 4–5 minutes, stirring, until browned. Season with the salt and pepper.
Add the onion, carrots and garlic and fry for 3 minutes, then the cabbage and pepper for 2 minutes more. Pour in the 300 ml water and bring to a simmer.

Lay the dough sheets over the meat and vegetables, folding them to fit, and cover tightly with the lid. Steam over medium-low heat for 12–15 minutes, until the dough is cooked through, firm and no longer sticky, and most of the liquid has been absorbed.
Lift the sheets onto a board and let them cool for 1–2 minutes. Roll each up loosely and slice into 5 mm wide noodles, then shake them apart.

Return the noodles to the pot and toss them with the meat and vegetables over medium-high heat for 3–4 minutes, until they have soaked up the juices and fried a little at the edges. Taste for salt (add the soy sauce, if using) and serve hot, with ketchup or chilli sauce and a pickled vegetable salad, as Mongolian canteens do.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: In a hurry, use 400 g fresh flat wheat noodles: cook them separately, then toss them with the meat and vegetables.

recipes.name: Khuushuur (Mongolian fried meat pastries)
recipes.description: Flat half-moon pastries filled with juicy minced lamb, onion and garlic, fried until blistered and golden. The essential snack of the summer Naadam festival.

ingredients.name: Lamb or mutton mince (or beef mince)

steps.t: Mix the flour, salt and water and knead for 5–8 minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 20 minutes.
Mix the mince with the onion, garlic, salt and pepper (and cumin, if using), then work in the cold water with your hand until the filling turns sticky. The water keeps the inside juicy as it fries.
Divide the dough into 12 pieces and roll each into a round about 12 cm across.

Spread 2 tablespoons of filling over one half of a round, leaving a 1 cm border. Fold the other half over to make a half-moon, press out the air and flatten the filling with your palm to an even thickness of about 1 cm so it cooks through in the time the pastry takes to brown. Seal the edge by pinching and folding it over itself into a rope pattern, or press it with a fork.

Heat 2 cm of oil in the frying pan to 170 °C. Fry 2–3 khuushuur at a time for 3–4 minutes per side, until deep golden and blistered and the filling is cooked through (71 °C; the juices bubble at the edges). Drain on the wire rack.
Serve hot, eaten with your hands, with a pickled cabbage or carrot salad and ketchup. At Naadam, people rub the hot pastries between their palms, which is said to be good for the hands.

recipes.storage: Freeze uncooked khuushuur between sheets of baking paper for 1 month; fry from frozen over slightly lower heat. Refrigerate cooked ones and eat within 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat on a rack in a 200 °C oven for 10 minutes until piping hot.

recipes.name: Thukpa (Tibetan noodle soup with beef)
recipes.description: A warming bowl of wheat noodles in a garlicky, gingery tomato broth with tender slices of beef, radish and greens, finished with coriander and a spoonful of chilli sauce.

ingredients.name: Dried wheat noodles (or fresh hand-made noodles)

steps.t: Toss the beef slices with the soy sauce and a pinch of salt and set aside while you prepare the vegetables.
Heat the oil in the large pot over medium-high heat and fry the onion for about 5 minutes, until soft and golden. Add the garlic, ginger and chilli and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes and ground yerma and cook for about 5 minutes, stirring and pressing, until the tomatoes have broken down into a thick base.
Add the beef and stir-fry for about 3 minutes, until browned all over.
Pour in the stock and bring to the boil. Simmer for 15 minutes, add the radish and simmer for 5 minutes more, until tender. Taste and season with salt.
Meanwhile cook the noodles in the second pot of boiling water until just tender, then drain. Cooking them separately keeps the broth clear rather than starchy.

Stir the spinach into the soup and cook for 1 minute until wilted. Divide the noodles between bowls, ladle the soup, beef and vegetables over and top with coriander and spring onion. Serve hot with a chilli sauce (sepen) to stir in.

recipes.storage: Keep the soup and noodles separately in the fridge for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Thukpa simply means noodle soup; Amdo and Lhasa families each have their own versions, and vegetarian thukpa uses vegetable stock with extra vegetables and tofu.

recipes.name: Thenthuk (Tibetan hand-pulled noodle soup)
recipes.description: Rustic soup of hand-torn flat noodles pulled straight into a simmering broth of lamb, tomato, radish and spinach. 'Then' means pull and 'thuk' means noodle.

steps.t: Mix the flour, salt and water and knead for about 8 minutes, until smooth and elastic. Divide it into 4 pieces, roll each into a log about 1.5 cm thick, coat with the oil and cover. Rest for at least 30 minutes: the relaxed gluten lets the dough stretch thin without snapping.

Heat the 2 tablespoons of oil in the large pot over medium-high heat. Fry the onion for 5 minutes until golden, add the garlic and ginger for 1 minute, then the tomatoes, and cook for 5 minutes until they break down.
Add the lamb and stir-fry for 3 minutes until browned, then add the radish and the stock. Bring to the boil and simmer for 15 minutes while you pull the noodles.

Pick up a dough log and flatten it between your fingers into a long ribbon about 3 cm wide and 3 mm thick. Holding it over the gently boiling soup, pinch off thumbnail-sized pieces, stretching each one slightly as you tear it, and drop them straight into the pot. Work quickly so the noodles cook evenly, stirring now and then so they don't stick together.
Once all the noodles are in, simmer for 3–5 minutes more, until they float and are cooked through and chewy, with no raw dough in the centre.

Stir in the spinach and soy sauce and cook for 1 minute until the spinach wilts. Season with salt and pepper, ladle into bowls and top with coriander and spring onion. Serve hot, with chilli sauce on the side.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat until steaming hot, adding a little water; the noodles soak up broth as they stand.

recipes.name: Tingmo (Tibetan steamed twisted bread)
recipes.description: Soft, fluffy steamed buns made by twisting oiled strips of yeasted dough into knots. Served warm with spicy stir-fries, curries and stews.

ingredients.name: Spring onions, finely chopped, for a savoury filling

steps.t: Stir the sugar and yeast into the warm water and leave for 5 minutes until foamy. Mix the flour, salt and baking powder in a bowl, pour in the yeast water and bring together into a dough.

Knead for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic: stretch the dough away from you with the heel of your hand, fold it back and turn it, repeating until it springs back when poked. Cover and leave in a warm place for 1–1½ hours, until doubled in size.

Punch down the dough and roll it into a rectangle about 3 mm thick. Brush generously with oil (and scatter with spring onion, if using). Fold it in half lengthwise and cut across into strips about 2 cm wide.

Take two strips together, stretch them gently to about twice their length, twist them like a rope and coil them into a round knot, tucking the ends underneath. The oil between the layers keeps the twists separate, giving tingmo its flower-like look. Set each on a square of baking paper.
Arrange the buns in the steamer with space between them, cover and leave to rise for 20 minutes, until puffy.
Steam over boiling water for 15 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave the lid on for 5 minutes before opening; a sudden rush of cold air makes steamed buns wrinkle and collapse.
Serve warm, pulling the layers apart, alongside shapta (spicy stir-fried beef), dal, curries or stews.

recipes.storage: Keep in a sealed bag for 1 day, or freeze for up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Steam for 5 minutes (8 from frozen) until soft and hot.

recipes.name: Po cha (Tibetan butter tea)
recipes.description: Strong black tea churned with butter, milk and salt into a smooth, frothy, savoury drink. Drunk throughout the day on the Tibetan plateau for warmth and energy.
equipment: Blender, stick blender or tall jug and whisk

ingredients.name: Strong black tea (from 2 tbsp loose black or brick tea boiled in 1 litre water)

steps.t: Put the tea leaves and 1 litre of water in the saucepan, bring to the boil and simmer for 5–10 minutes, until the tea is very dark. Tibetan households often keep a strong brick-tea concentrate simmering for hours and dilute it as needed.
Strain the tea into the blender or a tall jug, discarding the leaves. Add the butter, milk and salt.

Churn it: blend for 30 seconds, or work it with a stick blender or a vigorous whisk, until the butter has completely emulsified and the tea is pale, creamy and frothy with no oily slick on top. In Tibet this is done in a tall wooden churn called a chandong.
Pour it back into the pan and reheat gently until steaming, without letting it boil, which would split the butter out again.
Serve hot in small bowls and top them up often, as a Tibetan host would. Stir a spoonful of tsampa (roasted barley flour) into the last of the tea to make a quick, filling snack.

recipes.storage: Best freshly made. Refrigerate leftovers and drink within 1 day, reheating and churning again before serving.
notes: Salted butter works if you leave out the added salt; the tea should taste savoury, more like a broth than a sweet drink.

recipes.name: Lanzhou niu rou mian (Lanzhou beef noodle soup)
recipes.description: The Hui Muslim noodle soup of Lanzhou: a clear, gently spiced beef broth with white radish, thin slices of beef, red chilli oil and green coriander over wheat noodles.

ingredients.name: White radish (daikon)
ingredients.prep: peeled and sliced into thin squares

ingredients.name: Dried wheat noodles (or fresh hand-pulled noodles)
Black vinegar, to serve at the table

steps.t: Soak the beef in a large bowl of cold water for 1 hour, changing the water once, to draw out the blood. Lanzhou cooks judge the soup first by how clear it is, and this soaking is where clarity starts.
Put the beef in the stockpot, cover with fresh cold water and bring to the boil. Boil for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse the beef and the pot to remove all the grey scum.

Return the beef to the pot with the water, stock and ginger. Tie the spices in muslin or a spice bag and add them. Bring to the boil, skim carefully, then lower the heat until the surface barely trembles. Simmer, partly covered, for 2 hours, until the beef is tender. Never let it boil hard, which clouds the broth.

While the broth simmers, make the chilli oil: put the chilli flakes and a pinch of salt in a heatproof bowl, heat the oil until it shimmers and a flake sizzles instantly, then pour it over. It should foam and turn brick red. Leave to cool.

Lift out the beef and spice bag. Strain the broth through a fine sieve (lined with muslin for the clearest result) into a clean pan and season well with salt and the white pepper. Add the radish and simmer for 10 minutes, until translucent. Slice the cooled beef thinly across the grain.
Cook the noodles in plenty of boiling water until just tender, then drain. Lanzhou noodle shops pull the dough to order in different thicknesses; dried noodles of any width work at home.

Divide the noodles between deep bowls and ladle over the hot broth and radish. Top with the sliced beef, a spoonful of chilli oil, coriander and garlic shoots. Serve at once, with black vinegar at the table.

recipes.storage: Keep the broth, beef and noodles separately; broth and beef keep 3 days in the fridge or 3 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Locals describe a good bowl as 'one clear, two white, three red, four green, five yellow': clear broth, white radish, red chilli oil, green coriander and garlic shoots, and yellow noodles.
Beef bones (about 1 kg, blanched with the shank) give a richer broth and can replace the stock.
